inline.s: Zhang the Filial Son’s Discourse on Sweet Dew

I once read the Records of Those Beyond the World, which say that when Chaos first divided and human beings first appeared, their bodies possessed radiance, they flew at will, breathed the wind and drank the dew, and did not produce the five grains. Springs gushed and dew fell, congealing like fat, and it was called Earth’s Richness; its flavor resembled ghee. People ate it and found it sweet, craving it without satiety, and their bodies gradually grew heavy, so that they could no longer lift themselves. Thus Earth’s Richness thinned and the five grains came to be; once the five grains arose, Earth’s Richness vanished. People then ate grain, and the apertures of desire were bored open; the fire of craving was born. So the pure vapor grew dilute and the dew was no longer sweet, the springs no longer sweet wine. Only when a sage emperor or enlightened king appeared, whose virtue matched Heaven and who guarded the pure vapor, did sweet dew fall and sweet springs gush forth; then these were omens, auspicious signs, wonders and blessings. They answer in Heaven what they move in men. Seen in this light, what is auspicious today was the norm in antiquity; in the ages of Yao and Shun it came about many times. The three dynasties left no record, and the Spring and Autumn Annals do not mention it; only in the reign of Emperor Wu of the Western Han did it fall, and from that time it began to be used to name a year, and thereafter each age had it. In the eighth year of Hongwu of our Ming, the Sage Ancestor went to the Fasting Palace to sacrifice to the Supreme Ruler, and sweet dew fell on the pine tips of the Circular Mound, congealing on the branches and hanging down, its form like pearls, its sweetness like syrup. He then commanded the assembled ministers to gather and taste it, and ordered poems and essays composed to record it; so it was in the reign of Emperor Shizong as well. From this we know that the auspicious sign of sweet dew appears only in response to the virtue of a king, and I have never heard of its falling in the countryside. Now Zhang Mingqiu of Longshan, by his deep filial piety, moved sweet dew to fall on the scholar tree in his courtyard, fragrant and lovely beyond the common, and it did not disperse for a full ten days. How is this so? Let me try to discuss it. Filial piety is the warp of Heaven, the righteousness of Earth, the conduct of the people. When the virtue of filial piety is perfected, the vapor of centrality and harmony is nourished; when centrality and harmony are nourished, the pure vapor is guarded; when the pure vapor is guarded, the virtue of Heaven is matched; when the virtue of Heaven is matched, auspicious blessings respond. Therefore sweet dew falls and sweet springs gush. Now filial piety is one and the same; from the Son of Heaven down to the common man there is originally no second kind. Only, where the mind is complete and the vapor full, the response comes swiftly, and its lasting long or brief is likewise so. Therefore I say that there is much in Zhang’s filial piety that he himself does not know; that is why the auspicious response has lasted so long, while those who expound it have not yet reached the whole. Alas, the hearts of men have long been drowned. Yet no one lacks this form; having this form, no one lacks this nature. When the nature is fully realized, the virtue of filial piety is complete, and auspicious blessings respond. And if there are men like Zhang, in whom one filial son rises in the family, a hundred filial sons rise in the village, and thousands, myriads and millions rise in the nation and throughout the world, then men will not be less than sages, nor affairs less than those of antiquity, and the world and the state may be raised to the highest antiquity, all alike enjoying the bliss of Huaxu. I would then certainly say that all dew is sweet and all springs are sweet wine, and that one may drink and eat as one pleases, without waiting for songs of praise and full bellies. What need would there be, then, for auspicious responses?
A Discourse on the Style Name Buqian, “That Which Does Not Shift”

My disciple Liang Sixiang bowed his head and paid reverence, asking me to confer a style name upon him. I styled him Buqian, “That Which Does Not Shift,” taking the sense from Master Sengzhao’s treatise. In my youth I read the Zhaolun, and when I came to the lines “The whirlwind that lays low the mountains is ever still; the rivers that race onward do not flow; the dust motes that drift and dance do not move; the sun and moon that hang in the sky do not circle,” I was utterly at a loss as to what they pointed to. In the jiaxu year of Wanli, while on pilgrimage, I reached Hezhong and spent the winter with my fellow student Miaofeng at the Shanyin Way-Court. There I collated and printed this treatise, and suddenly had an opening into it. When I lifted the blind and saw the wind blowing the leaves of the trees, so that they fluttered and filled the air, I bore witness to it myself and said, “Master Sengzhao truly did not deceive me.” Whenever I raised this before others, they all said, “Within movement there is that which does not move.” I laughed and said, “If so, then it is the principle that does not move, not what Sengzhao meant by ‘things do not shift.’ Yet since he says ‘even things do not shift,’ how could he set aside things to seek the principle, or discard movement to seek stillness?” Master Liang’s personal name is Sixiang, the Four Marks; yet there is no thing that is not shifted by these four marks, and that which is not shifted is not something ordinary feeling can fathom or know. Sengzhao alone saw it through to the heart. Now that Master Liang has turned his mind toward the Dharma-gate, does he not have aspiration for this? If he attains the wonder of that which does not shift, then in his daily life before his eyes — in all the movement and stillness, leisure and bustle; in adversity and compliance, suffering and joy; in gain and loss, toil and ease; in profit and decline, slander and praise; even in wealth and honor, poverty and lowliness; and in the greatest matters of calamity and birth and death — he will not perceive the slightest mark of coming or going. Then Śākyamuni’s manifestation-bodies, Guanyin’s responsive appearances, and Samantabhadra’s myriad practices of adornment — indeed all mundane and supramundane dharmas — are drained in a single draught; how much more, then, would he appear in the body of a magistrate to teach the Dharma? Seen in this light, Yao and Shun used it to rule with folded hands, Yi Yin and Lü Shang used it to save the people, Yan Hui used it with his basket and gourd, and it is why Confucius was at ease wherever he went. The Master, standing by a river, said, “What passes away is like this, never resting day or night.” Alas, those words of the Master are truly a wooden bell in the long night’s dream. Sengzhao drew them out and extended them, and this old man takes this character to name Master Liang. If he can be worthy of these words, he may be called a true son of the sage’s gate — how much more of the Dharma-gate.
A Discourse on the Style Name of Huang Yongzhong

The scholar Huang Yuanheng: I styled him Yongzhong, “Using the Mean,” and have made this discourse for him. Now the Mean has no substance of its own — how can it be used? Yet viewed by means of the steelyard, the Mean becomes visible of itself. For the steelyard is that by which all under Heaven is leveled, the standard of the ten thousand things, which men must trust, and which can be understood without words. What a pity that men know the steelyard to be trustworthy, yet do not know that its use of the Mean lies here. It is like ordinary people who know that food satisfies hunger, but do not know that what satisfies is the flavor; they take the flavor lightly and their food is coarse. Hence it is said, “Only the refined, only the one; truly hold fast to the Mean.” Not knowing the flavor, one does not know refinement; not knowing the Mean, one is not good at using it. Only one who can use the Mean may be said to make great use of it. Let Master Huang remember this.
A Discourse on the Style Name of Ou Jiake

The scholar Ou Xingji came from afar to visit me. Young as he is, he is diligent and hardworking, and I admired his resolve on meeting him; so I styled him Jiake, “Worthy of Approval.” Now whenever we say “may” or “acceptable,” we gloss it as “barely acceptable”; and “barely” implies something not yet complete — which is wrong. A man desires something in his mind: if it is acceptable he craves it, if not he rejects it, and the cravings of his mind do not cease until they are exhausted; there are even those who, though their desires are exhausted, still do not stop. How can this be called “merely”? Thus men of every age, though they dwell within the acceptable, do not know that it is acceptable. It is only the Chan gate, on the road that goes beyond, that uses mind to seal mind, and that is called the seal of approval. In a sage it is said, “There is nothing that is not acceptable”; and one for whom nothing is unacceptable has nothing that is unacceptable. Hence for all the people and all things in the world, for the age and the times, for the times and fate, there is a sure and unshifting acceptance. If one knows this unshifting Way, then failure and success are one horizon, danger and safety one measure, withdrawal and service one moment; and being so, nothing is unacceptable. If a man can see this acceptance clearly, then wherever he goes he will find his own place. Let Master Ou know that this juncture is called the ultimate reality; and is ultimate reality a small matter?
A Discourse on the Style Name Shixiu, “The Scholar’s Cultivation”

The scholar Zheng Shangzhi asked me for a style name. I styled him Shixiu. For when a man sets his will on the Way, without cultivation he cannot fulfill the Way. Yet the Way is in us, complete from the outset, lacking nothing and with nothing to spare; it is only because things and desires block and cover it that we lose what we originally have, so that the six apertures plunder one another and the six officers fail in their duties. This is what the foolish and unworthy fall short of. Even among those who have aspiration, the worthy may overdo it in practice and the clever may overdo it in understanding; therefore the sages take the middle course, restraining what goes too far and drawing out what falls short, bringing it back to the great mean and perfect uprightness, so as to complete what one originally has and not lose one’s heavenly innocence. This is what is called cultivation — it is not that apart from this there is some other cultivation. Hence it is said, “Cultivating the Way is called teaching.” From this we know that when the sages taught others, they did not add anything to them; they only fashioned them according to what they had been endowed with, and drew them out according to what they aspired to. Thus even in the midst of daily seeing, hearing, perceiving and knowing, and within rising and resting, eating and breathing, there is nowhere that is not the ground where one’s original brightness stands alone revealed. But because of long habit it is obstructed; therefore one uses what is already clear to penetrate what is obscured. As the eye is obstructed by forms, one penetrates it through forms; as the ear is obstructed by sounds, one penetrates it through sounds; as the tongue is obstructed by flavors, one penetrates it through flavors; as the nose is obstructed by scents, one penetrates it through scents; as the body is obstructed by contacts, one penetrates it through contacts; as the mind is obstructed by knowing, one penetrates it through knowing. One washes away old habit and brings out one’s original brightness, as when a mirror is polished: once the grime is gone the brightness appears. Yet the mirror’s brightness is originally there; it is not increased by polishing and washing. Because what he practices is the Way, one uses that resolve to open it. If he has no single-minded and unshakable resolve, he will surely be carried off by habitual defilement, drifting daily into confusion, far astray and not knowing how to return, and will no longer deserve to be called a man — how much less be fit to be called a scholar? Therefore I say: the scholar prizes aspiration, and aspiration prizes cultivation. This is the discourse for Shixiu.
A Discourse on the Style Name of Xu Zihou

The scholar Xu Tianzai bowed and asked for a style name. I styled him Zihou, “Master Depth.” And I have made this discourse for him. Heaven is what our nature is in itself; and as for speaking of “bearing,” the meaning is that the nature is able to bear things. The Transmission says, “Bring centrality and harmony to their utmost: Heaven and Earth take their places, and the ten thousand things are nourished.” For centrality is the substance of the nature, and harmony is its virtue. If we can bring our nature to its utmost, then the substance is complete and the virtue is vast, and we can set Heaven and Earth in their places and nourish the ten thousand things. This is simply what is inherent in the nature. Yet although the nature is originally complete, if it is not nourished it cannot reach the utmost of the vast and fulfill the finest. Therefore I have taken for him the word “depth,” intending that he deepen his nourishment and make his depth weighty, so that he can bear and sustain without letting anything fall. Hence it is said, “If the wind is not piled deep, it has no strength to bear great wings; if the water is not piled deep, it has no strength to bear a great ship.” Now our nature and its virtue, complete in us, are vast by nature; yet unless one accumulates nourishment deep and thick, one has no strength to bear a great burden. For this reason the heroic men of old who were endowed with extraordinary talent all toiled and sharpened their resolve, tempering their keen tools, to await the great use of the world and the state, and to establish great works that would not decay for a thousand years — which is how they lit up a hundred generations and let their bounty flow without end, the source far and the stream long, depth at its utmost. Because the nature is the root of Heaven, Earth and the ten thousand things, one who can fulfill the nature may stand as a third with Heaven and Earth, and only then does he exhaust a great man’s work. When his work is done, he may be called a man; otherwise he rots away like any object — how then be called a great man? Therefore the sages dwell in depth and not in shallowness, in the solid and not in the flowery; to leave the flowery and take the solid is the Way of depth. So I styled him Zihou. Let him exert himself.
A Discourse on the Style Name Rongwo, “That Which Contains Me”

Heaven and Earth are vast beyond measure, and there is nothing the ten thousand things do not contain. Yet he says, “Contain me” — could it be that I alone cannot find room? Still, there must be an explanation. A man of old said, “Who says Heaven and Earth are broad? Beyond the gate there is only obstruction.” So there are indeed those who find no room; it is not that Heaven and Earth cannot contain me, but that I cannot find room within Heaven and Earth. Therefore the sage embraces the ten thousand things without making them his own; not making them his own is no-self. With no-self there is no thing; with no thing there is nothing to oppose; with nothing to oppose, things and self are forgotten; things and self forgotten, all things are self; all things are self, and the self merges with the ten thousand things. Because he is merged and one with them, he can contain me. This is the sage’s accomplishment; only one who has forgotten contrivance resembles him. Therefore I give this as the style name of Elder Li.
A Discourse on the Style Name Xie Ruzhong

The boy of Zhanggong is named Shangjia. He asked me for a style name, and I styled him Ruzhong, “Your Loyalty”: it means shifting filial devotion into loyalty, which is indeed what the “Above” in his name approves. The boy was born in a bing year, and the fire of bing figures the virtue of a ruler — bright and firm and upright, firm without and soft within: the substance of virtue. Hence it is called “soft and fine.” It means that yang is firm and yin is soft, that the ruler is firm and the minister soft; this is the uprightness of high and low and the harmony of Heaven and Earth. The great comes and the small departs; yang seeks yin, yin enters yang. Hence in the trigrams it is li, fire; in man it is the heart and the eye. The essence of the heart overflows into the eyes, and what the eyes see is governed by the heart: inner and outer are one. Thus the ruler’s seeking of the minister is as the heart’s relation to the eye, and the minister’s service of the ruler is as the eye’s relation to the heart. So inner and outer are one and their function is not divided; virtue joins and merit is accomplished — and so he may be approved. Otherwise he is in peril. It is what is called seeing with the ears and hearing with the eyes: then the heavenly ruler loses his watch and the five officers fail in their duties, and to seek approval — would that not be hard? From this we know that when a minister serves his ruler as the eye obeys the heart’s command, that is loyalty at its utmost. Therefore I take his “approved” and approve it the more, for loyalty is indeed worthy of approval. I observe that the boy is spirited and his frame is noble, his temper harmonious and his mind at peace — the stuff of a great man. The saying goes, “The great man is one who does not lose the heart of a newborn child.” In truth he bears beforehand the signs of a great man, already visible in his bearing, countenance, frame and appearance. Was not Confucius at play arranging sacrificial vessels and setting out the forms of ritual — was this not something Heaven conferred, which he then brought to completion as a man? His teacher, in this month, is sending the boy up to the elementary school, and has given him this name. I have styled him Yizhong. His teacher wishes me to write this out and keep it safe, to be the boy’s left tally, as it were.
A Discourse on the Style Name Juezhi, “Awakening”

Master Fang Yimin followed his father on official travels to Heng and paid me reverence, asking about the supramundane Dharma; he then asked for a Dharma name. I named him Fuxin, “Blessing-Mind,” because the mind is the root of the field of blessing and that to which all good returns, like rich soil that produces a hundred grains. He then asked for a style name, and I styled him Juezhi, “Awakening”: for Buddha means the awakened. An old worthy said, “This very mind is Buddha.” Because this mind is originally Buddha, and because of delusion one becomes a sentient being — this is the transformation of awakening into delusion. In our daily life, with the single thought before us: if we are awake, one thought is a Buddha; if thought after thought we are always awake, we are the eternally abiding Buddha. If we are not awake, we fall forever into delusion and lose what we originally have, like a man with eyes who sits in a dark room and sees nothing — one who is, as it is said, confused and unawakened. Since the mind is the field of blessing and awakening is the seed, then to be unwakeful in daily life is to have a field and not plow it; how can one hope for a harvest? Therefore I say: awaken. Awakening is the root of planting blessings. If Master Fang can awaken, he will not betray what he originally has, and that is the greatest of blessings.
Reading Master Da’s Discourse on the Style Name Dongwen

As for the words of Dongwen, they follow Wenshu’s selection of the perfect penetration, taking Guanyin’s ear-root as supreme, and further take Samantabhadra’s “the mind hears and penetrates the ten directions” as the standard. One takes the ear as perfect, the other takes the mind as penetrating. But as for old Han’s part in it, he sees empty space knotted together with an eyebrow, and the ten thousand things all heard; then the three great beings would be left speechless with a single “hmph,” and Zibo’s words too would have nowhere to lodge. Only one who penetrates through at this point may be called one who has heard through the cave.
Changing the Style Name of the Hall Master Tianxiang to Wuyin

The hall master Ming Gui had the old style name Tianxiang, “Heavenly Fragrance,” and asked old man Haiyin to change it, since it had grown close to the commonplace. The old man laughed and answered, “A name is a borrowed name, and the real cannot be named at all; whatever can be named is commonplace.” And so the matter was dropped. One day the master happened to come to the abbot’s quarters and said, “Last night in a dream I saw you change my style name, and when I asked what it was, I had forgotten it.” The old man laughed again and said, “Birth and death, nirvāṇa — all are like last night’s dream; and whatever can be named or styled is dream-talk. One who well knows all dharmas to be like dreams finds that all names and words are nothing but dream matters. If one contemplates dharmas as dream, the Buddha-dharma is always present.” So he named him Wuyin, “Nothing Hidden,” taking the sense of what is plain before the eyes: where the six faculties meet their objects, there is nothing that is not Buddha-work. Consider how Lingyun saw a peach blossom and awakened to the Way, and how Xiangyan heard a bamboo struck and clarified his mind; both realized the truth right at the gate of sound and form. And the Daoist of Shangu, relying on Master Hutang, begged him to point out the shortcut. Hutang said, “Take Confucius’ words: ‘Do you think, my disciples, that I conceal anything from you? I conceal nothing from you.’ How do you ordinarily reason about this, Your Excellency?” The master was about to answer, and Hutang said, “No, no.” One day, as he attended Hutang walking in the hills, the rock osmanthus was in full bloom. Hutang asked, “Do you smell the fragrance of the osmanthus?” He said, “I do.” Hutang said, “I conceal nothing from you.” Shangu was set free, and bowed at once, saying, “How earnestly the master’s grandmotherly heart works!” This is a case of a common fellow entering realization through the dust of fragrance. Let not the hall master say that one who enters by the dust of fragrance may be styled Wuyin; is there anything else that is hidden? Confucius also said, “There is no one who acts with me without my showing it to you: that is Qiu.” Contemplate this.
A Discourse on the Style Name Xuhuai, “Empty Bosom”

In the year wuwu, the year after the parinirvāṇa of Great Master Zhulin of Mount Wutai, his disciple Daqian came from afar to Mount Kuang and asked me to compose his pagoda inscription. The master had studied in the capital at Biyun Temple on the Western Hills. Biyun was a famed monastery of the royal city, and the abundance of its four requisites made it foremost among monks for enjoying the finest pleasures of desire. Yet the master could abandon this and go into the cold cliffs and ice and snow to draw near to good friends and devote his mind to the Buddha-dharma. Zhulin’s disciples numbered in the thousands, yet he alone set his mind on imperishable radiance in his final hour. His regard for the root is thus evident. When I sat and talked with him and sounded what he held within, I found him wholly devoted to contemplation of principle and scrupulous in upholding the precepts, so that the direction he tended was not to be compared with the busy traffickers in worldly truth. I admired him greatly. His former style name was Yuguang, “Brighter Yet,” and I disliked its dazzle; so I changed it to Xuhuai, taking the sense that an empty mind can receive benefit. For sentient beings lie long in the sleep of birth and death without waking simply because they are sunk in the five desires and their accumulated habits are thick, so that vexation fills their breasts; hence everything they do becomes fuel for karma. Because they grasp and do not transform what they have, their accumulated grime grows deeper; the deeper the grime, the heavier the karma; delusion piles on delusion and the road of suffering grows longer, with never a turn to look back. What radiance can there be? Tracing it to its cause, the fault lies in the mind’s not being empty. The sage empties himself and wanders in the world because he can let go of what he grasps; when what he grasps is let go, the mind is empty of itself; when the mind is empty, objects are still of themselves. Mind empty and objects still, self and things are both forgotten; when the self is forgotten there is no mind to grasp, and when things are forgotten the grasped objects are cut off. Then mind and objects, sought, are utterly unattainable: emptiness at its utmost. With a bosom like this he stands apart and wanders with the Way. What single thing could bind him, what mote of dust weary him? Yet entering the nothing with the nothing, his wondrous practice tallies in the dark; he throws his body in for the sake of things — what is called “not rising from the cessation-samādhi yet manifesting all deportments.” This is the accomplishment of the consummate man in the world; how could it stop at modest humility? It is radiance that does not dazzle.
A Discourse on the Style Name of Nie Yingru

The scholar Nie studied under Chan Master Daguan, who styled him Yingru, “He Ought to Be Thus.” Observing his style name, I know what the master conferred upon him to be the highest Dharma-gate; and so I make this discourse for him. Now “thus” is not a matter of resemblance; it points directly at our own original substance. What is called true suchness is another name for the one mind. Being true, it is not false; being thus, it does not change: hence true suchness. Because this mind is luminous and vast, clear as empty space, its substance is still. Even as the sun goes and the moon comes, dark and bright alternate, clouds move and birds fly, the wind stirs and dust rises, the four seasons revolve and day and night leave no gap, and all such transformations arise and cease without pause — the substance of emptiness remains still and unmoving. We are endowed with this true-suchness nature and rely on it for our bodily form, yet we are carried off by false thinking; honor and disgrace, worry and delight, love and hate, joy and anger, illness and calamity, and even the succession of birth and death — all such transformations become obstructions. So the substance is originally thus, and now it is not thus. Therefore the Chan master, following what is inherently his, guides him, saying, “You ought to be thus.” Hence “Yingru”: because one is originally self-such, yet now is not such; and if one wishes to recover what one originally has, there is no need to seek outside — one need only be thus. If one is such as one’s original suchness, what further suchness is there? From this we know that sage and ordinary are not separated in us; it all lies in the interval between delusion and awakening, between being such and not being such. Not such, one is ordinary; such, one is a sage. The Prajñā says, “What is called Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas.” Seen in this light, not only is the substance of the mind originally such; all dharmas are such. Taken near, in one’s own person, the four elements and six faculties, and finely peeled apart, the thirty-six substances, are all such within and without. Taken far, in external things, mountains and rivers and the great earth, scaly and shelled, feathered and furred, grasses and trees and fine dust, and to the very limit all the forms and marks in the world, are none of them not such. Hence it is said, “The green, green bamboo is all true suchness; the lush, lush yellow flowers are nothing but prajñā.” Viewed thus, all dharmas are of themselves thus; and all dharmas being thus, what is there to like or dislike, to grasp or reject, and be held back and obstructed by the karma of birth and death? It is as said: the ten thousand objects are originally at leisure; it is men who make the noise. If a man turns things, he is the same as the Tathāgata. When things are turned, mind and objects are both such, self and things are both forgotten, sage and ordinary are equal, and birth and death, coming and going, are like a dream, like an illusion — what have they to do with our numinous awareness? Therefore we who have the aspiration to leave birth and death ought to be thus. Hence “Yingru.” Let him remember this.
A Discourse on the Style Name of He Xiyou

The scholar He is styled Xiyou, “How Rare.” He is firmly set on the Way; and that a man can face the Way is indeed rare. If he can truly see the Way, that is rarer still. I once read the Diamond Sutra, and when I came to where Subhūti sighed before the World-Honored One, saying, “How rare!” I was much perplexed. Then I looked back to before his sigh, and found nothing remarkable there, and no profound words either: only that the World-Honored One put on his robe, took up his bowl, ate his meal, walked on, washed his feet and sat down. There was nothing else remarkable. What did Subhūti see that made him exclaim in wonder like that? For a thousand years and more, patriarchs and Buddhas have annotated these words without breaking through them; then suddenly Subhūti saw through the place of the World-Honored One’s conduct, and could not keep from crying out. What has Master He, Xiyou, actually seen, that he should find it rare? Suppose he sees through the place where Subhūti saw through the World-Honored One, and sees through his own household — these are merely the everyday matters of getting through daily life. What dharma, then, would he point to as a rare dharma, what matter as a rare matter? If he has not yet set his eye on it, but merely contends in praise and admiration over the marks of words, I fear that when one day he turns his head for a look, he will find it not so rare after all. Master He begged for a Dharma-word; since this old man has no dharma to speak, I therefore speak this in accord with his request.
A Discourse on the Style Name Xianglin, “Fragrant Grove”

The Elder Cishan of Dadu is named Zhenxiao, “True Filial Piety.” Master Da styled him Xianglin, “Fragrant Grove,” and asked me to make a discourse for him. When I was in Wuyang, I saw Western ocean-going ships bring sandalwood, and I asked where it grew. They said it grows in a land of fragrance, a land most poisonous and hot and full of huge serpents. The serpents’ own venom is so hot that nothing can relieve it; only by relying on this fragrant wood can they relieve it, and so they coil about it to gain coolness; and because of the serpents’ venom the fragrance of the wood is all the richer. Moreover the tree grows alone; where it grows no other grasses grow, and its fragrance alone forms a grove. Hence the old worthy said, “Within sandalwood all common timber is cut off.” Now Master Da uses the Fragrant Grove to praise filial piety; surely the name is not without meaning. Our original teacher Śākyamuni appeared in the world and taught the three studies of precepts, samādhi and wisdom, with special devotion to the precepts. Of the categories of precept there are very many, and among them the great Brahmā Net precepts are supreme. These precepts are the Dharma taught to bodhisattvas; without a vajra mind one cannot uphold them. I observe that in the sutra’s chapter on the precepts, filial piety is taken as the root. Hence the sutra says, “Filial piety is called the precepts”: to be filial to father and mother, filial to teachers and the Three Jewels, filial to the Dharma of the utmost Way, filial to all sentient beings. And the Vinaya records the categories of precept, roughly listing five hundred, and in detail the three thousand deportments and eighty thousand fine practices; yet the Buddha singles out the word “filial piety” as the root. His meaning is that if a Buddha’s child can fulfill this filial piety, then all the categories of precept are complete in a single mind. Is this not like sandalwood growing alone? When the three poisons’ burning fever scorches body and mind and there is no relief, only by relying on the precepts does one gain coolness — is this not like sandalwood’s power to dispel the great venom of serpents? Filial piety is born in the fevered mind-ground of sentient beings, and its own substance is pure so as to dissolve affliction; as affliction presses, the light of the precepts becomes perfect. Is this not like sandalwood growing in a land of venomous heat, itself cool, and by means of that venomous heat completing its fragrance? When one filial piety is complete, all precepts are fulfilled; when the precepts are fulfilled, filial piety becomes all the truer — like a grove of sandalwood. Hence “Fragrant Grove.” To make this his name — is it not fitting? This is Master Da’s teaching without teaching; my discourse is superfluous.
A Discourse on the Style Name Jianbai, “Firm and White”

Master Shou is abbot in the capital, with a noble aspiration toward the higher and a love of drawing near to good friends. Though he has not wandered through a hundred cities, yet whenever a renowned elder of good conduct from any quarter arrived, he rejoiced in them all — one might call it “sitting in attendance.” Formerly he drew near to my Dharma-brother, Master Gumei, who esteemed him deeply and once styled him Jianbai, “Firm and White.” Therefore I make this discourse for him. The Buddha-nature in the toils of affliction is like a maṇi jewel fallen into filth, like a lotus in the mud: it is not darkened by the defilement of affliction, not soiled by the silt of the five desires, for its own nature is spontaneously thus, originally pure, luminous and spotless as this. Yet men, seeing the filth, do not know the maṇi’s radiance; seeing the mud, they do not know the lotus’s fragrant purity. So they churn on in the dust of toil, not knowing the perfect brightness of their own nature. The master grew up amid the dust, yet stands out with the aspiration to leave it; his mind longs for the Pure Land and he wearies of birth and death. This is indeed the single thought standing alone in brightness, ever illumining as conditions arise. He will make the dust of toil itself into Buddha-work and turn a defiled land into a Pure Land; how could he be measured merely by “firm and white, same and different”? Still, resolve is not firm unless it is ground, and the mind is not white unless it is washed. Our resolve is ground firm by patience, and the mind is washed white by the precepts. If patience reaches the unborn and the precepts return to self-nature, and self-nature is pure, that is what is called “ground but not worn away.” If ground and not worn away, then dyed but not blackened. Firm means undecaying; white means unchanging. Undecaying and unchanging, true reality abides forever. Is this not the meaning of the Pure Land of Measureless Life? If the master truly contemplates his own mind by my words, then the thing in his bosom will appear before him, and he will not have failed his good friends. Otherwise he fails not only others but himself as well. Let him exert himself. This is the discourse.
A Discourse on Self-Nature

I have said that what rules a man from birth is the nature; the nature is one, yet its grades are not one, and this is why there is a distinction between sages and worthies. It comes from the difference between those who know by birth, those who know by learning, and those who know through hardship, and from the thickness or thinness of their habits, so that accomplishment is easy or hard. Sages who know by birth are not seen in every age; those who know by learning or through hardship — it is precisely a matter of the thickness or thinness of habit. Hence it is said, “By nature they are near; by habit they grow far.” Is this not the meaning? Most of us stand on the ground of learning, and the work we put forth need not be sought by galloping outward; we should know that self-nature is the master and put our strength there. If one cannot suddenly see the self-nature, one should examine the thickness or thinness of habitual tendencies, cutting and polishing, and put strength at the root. It is like polishing a mirror: once the dust and grime are removed, the brightness appears of itself. For us, in daily practice, there is no simpler or more urgent method than this. Hence it is said, “The essential of learning the Way is only to cure habit; when habit is exhausted, the nature is of itself fulfilled.” For the self-nature is originally bright, and admits of no increase; it is only that human desire obscures it, with greed, hatred, delusion and craving as its seeds, and one wallows in them and is trapped. So we know that “trapped” here is not the trapping of poverty: it is being trapped by bad habits. Confucius said, “He was not trapped by wine” — this is but one instance of being trapped. In every life there is more than one kind of trap. One who is not trapped by any obstruction may be called a person of great strength. Therefore the student of the Way must first of all possess a bold and hardy root and bone, like one man matching ten thousand, much like Li Guang riding alone in and out of the caitiff’s court. If we can go in and out with a single blade amid the fields of sound and form, goods and profit, and the desires of things, we deserve to be called a heroic and bold great man. To speak of learning in this way: simply where one is not trapped, one sees the self-nature; it is not that apart from being trapped there is some other work of seeking learning and knowing. That is why the Chan school speaks of “becoming Buddha standing on the spot” — it is simply suddenly seeing the self-nature; it is not that there is another Buddha to become. Buddha means the awakened: one’s own originally possessed luminous awakened nature. If one can see this nature, one is on the spot a sage. At this point one no longer sees any difference between knowing by birth, by learning, or through hardship; this is the work of fulfilling the nature. Once this nature is fulfilled, then in serving one’s ruler one is truly loyal, in serving one’s parents truly filial, in dealing with friends truly trustworthy, in the relation of husband and wife truly harmonious; and when extended to the world and the state, whatever one does, every affair and every dharma, becomes imperishable merit and work. What is called great merit and illustrious name has no other art: it comes from being true. In the winter of the jiyou year my boat lay on the Furong River. Master Li Hanli came to visit, and I saw his countenance and bearing clear as ice and jade, warm, generous and gentle: it is because for many lives he has played his mind in the ground of the nature and worn away his habitual tendencies, and so it shows thus in his outward bearing. If from this he advances without ceasing in effort, until he reaches the ground where selfish desire is wholly exhausted, sage and worthy will arrive without being sought. As for fame and worldly achievement, they are as echo answers sound, as shadow follows form, no more than the spittle left over. Hence it is said, “The truth of the Way is for governing the self; its leftover strands serve the world and the state.” All of it is the true radiance of the self-nature, not a matter apart. Let him keep this in mind.
The Dream-Wanderings of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Forty
A Memorial for Making a Sandalwood Image of Mañjuśrī on Mount Wutai

I bow before the truth that the surpassing realm of Qingliang is the way-place of ten thousand sages, and that great Wisdom Mañjuśrī is the teacher and model of the seven Buddhas. His traces have descended upon the land of the dawn; his Way transforms the Sahā world. He is the field of blessing for sentient beings, opening the eyes of gods and men. For those who take refuge in him, blessing equals the sands of the Ganges; for those who revere and praise him, merit exceeds the dust of kalpas — how much more for those who carve his form and cast his image and adorn them with offerings? I, a mountain monk, have presumptuously taken on the robe and form and been blessed to shelter on the numinous mountain, dwelling at the highest ridge of the Central Peak and opening a Brahmā-monastery of the ten directions. Moved by the Great Being’s awesome radiance and tearing apart the net of karma from many lives, I have therefore aroused the mind and vow to make one image of the Bodhisattva in sandalwood, asking that it be placed on this mountain for offerings. Then I came south to Yue, and three autumns have passed. I journeyed south shadowed only by myself, over a road of ten thousand li. I am ashamed that my blessing is light and my conditions thin, the matter weighty and the man mean; and so time slipped by in delay, and to this day I have not achieved an inch of result. Now I am fortunate to meet the surpassing assembly at Nanhua and to rely on the Sixth Patriarch’s compassionate light to gather the eminent men of the four assemblies and bind the good fruit of the ten directions. I humbly pray that noble officials and elders, men of understanding and famous men, will at once open the eye of wisdom and split open the purse of stinginess: to give one inch of incense from the heart, whose worth is three thousand, and to adorn one hair of the Dharma-body, whose blessing extends through ten thousand kalpas. If many together accomplish the thirty-two marks, then a hundred thousand million bodies will appear at once. Thus everyone will return to the golden realm, and each will be perfumed alike with the fragrance of prajñā. The merit is beyond thought; the conditions of blessing are without measure. I reverently set forth this memorial.
A Memorial Soliciting Grain for the Monastic Meals at Xiaofu Garden West of Canton

I hold firmly that one may leave the dust and depart from the common without its mattering that one’s traces are still bound among men, and that borrowing the false to cultivate the true gives one the confidence that the mind transcends the world. Yet since the five elements are present in the body, the four requisites must be provided for; and being unable to move gods and men, one must look up and rely on donors. I, a mountain monk, have hung up my staff outside the walls of Wuyang and cultivate in hiding within Xiaofu Garden. At the six periods I revere and recite, and have carved the lotus of the White Society; in the three karmas I am diligent, unfolding the palm-leaf scriptures of the Green Grove. Only, having sealed off conditions for so long, I have met with a lean year: noble and base share the calamity, worthy and foolish suffer one kalpa. The gates are shut for days on end, and alone I watch the earthen pot gather dust; I sit stiffly for ten days at a stretch, and who asks that the fragrant kitchen has run out of grain? Since I cannot beg for alms by the rule, I cannot avoid going around the district. Therefore, grudging no toil of a thousand li, I widely call upon the elders of the ten directions. May they happily give rise to joy and greatly shatter their stinginess. From a single grain to a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand grains, together piling up Mount Sumeru; from one man leading a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand men straight to the treasure-land. Turning morsels of food into the food of Dharma, the merit is beyond measure; turning fevered affliction into coolness, the field of blessing is without end. May the vajra seeds be scattered widely among gods and men, and may the ship of prajñā carry all alike to the other shore. Accept adversity as it comes and take it smoothly; go empty and return full. If one can return with a full load, one will not have failed to come at the news of it. If a surpassing condition can be met, such a good assembly is not common. May each follow his own arousal of mind; surely nothing given is cast away. I reverently set forth this memorial.
A Memorial for Making a Buddha Image in Sandalwood

I bow before the truth that the Dharma-body is without marks and relies on marks to make the mind clear, and that wondrous practice is non-doing yet lies precisely in doing, whereby one sees the truth. If one did not borrow the false to cultivate the true, how could one turn the ordinary into the sage? Our Tathāgata appeared in the world and taught without fixed method, forsaking himself to follow others and benefiting beings according to conditions. He established his teaching at Vulture Peak and opened the Udumbara’s peerless blossom; he left his model in Jambudvīpa and carved the auspicious image in sandalwood. Thus he brought it about that those who see and hear and look up in reverence all leave the road of delusion, and that those who revere, invoke and take refuge all ascend to the treasure-land. From the time the golden light shone eastward and the white horse came from the west, men have aroused their minds at the sight of the teaching of images and used adornment to express the Dharma. That is why jeweled palaces fill the land of China and dark-blue images crowd the garden of Jetavana. Those who revere them range from the Son of Heaven down to the common man; those who awaken to the Way include kings and lords and reach even to the various kinds of beings. All spread gold in earnest devotion and cut off their attachments to pour out their sincerity. Of the eighty-four thousand doors of practice, making blessing is the first. Of the four hundred and eighty temples of the Southern Dynasties, Lingyin stands foremost. The mountain flew here from the Western Regions; the apes were called out at the mouth of the cave. The setting equals Tuṣita; its surpassing beauty exceeds the human world. I, a mountain monk, left the dust and common life early and took shelter on a famous mountain. I delight in the pure cultivation of a quiet aranya and set my will on the ascetic practices of a dhūta. But since my faculties are inferior, I have not matched the Supreme Vehicle; and so I look up to the noble spirit of the Lotus Society and imitate the old story of King Udayana. I reverently carve a fragrant sandalwood image and install it for offering in the bodhi way-place, using it to fumigate and cultivate and relying on it for pure karma. The image is one foot six inches high, representing the sixteen-foot Dharma-body; I widely call upon the ten directions to plant the Buddha-seed of the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Yet though each person is himself Buddha, one must see the Buddha to arouse the mind; and though each has the conditions, one must meet the conditions to accomplish it. I, a mountain monk, grudging no ten thousand li, have come far to Wuyang, trudging through hardship and toiling wearily. This southern Yue is a famous region beyond the ranges, where rare treasures all gather, a dense forest of merchants, its hills and waters rich and winding, truly a gathering-place of letters. Moreover this surpassing merit requires no great outlay. How could there be no heroic spirits to take it up whole, no bold great men to shoulder it entirely? From one man to persuade ten or a hundred, many hands make light work; from one share to a hundred or a thousand, gathered small it becomes great. Though one Buddha transforms many people, each of those many becomes a Buddha. I humbly pray that noble officials and elders, men of understanding and lofty station, will all give rise to joy and each arouse a sincere mind, and straightway break open the purse of stinginess, not letting the moment pass before their eyes. Give away the floating clouds outside the body and make the true Buddha of your own mind. If one can for a single thought consent to turn the light and shine back, one will see the forty-eight wondrous marks, dignified and grave; the udumbara blossom will appear again in three thousand worlds, and the fruit of bodhi will leap beyond vast kalpas in an instant. The merit is not set in vain; the blessing is not wasted. Only resolve in faith without doubt and ascend straight to the treasure-land.
A Memorial for Repairing the Patriarchs’ Pagoda at Nanhua Temple

The adornment of a Buddha-land, though it be the good fruit of gods and men, and the giving that makes a Pure Land, is precisely the root of prajñā. If one does not trace the fruit back to its cause, one must seek the field and sow the seed. Look only at the affairs of the world before you: how could it be that I do the work and another reaps? Why toil to seek beyond your share? Surely it is by one’s own cultivation that one gains. A thousand years of fields and land — men say they have had eight hundred owners. When the three inches of breath are gone, one begins to regret that a whole life was spent in vain. How much better the true body of the Sixth Patriarch, which to this day has not decayed. The ten directions’ permanent abode — one should know that through kalpas it is not worn away. Incense smoke fills the sky, revealing the radiance of the self-nature; the jeweled pagoda towers into space, manifesting the Pure Land that is only mind. Yet since mist and clouds are illusion and transformation, who can keep his refined form for a whole life? Wind and rain ravage it, and at once the bases of the pillars are seen to rot. If one does not seize the time and rescue it urgently, I truly fear it cannot be held up another day. If one can remove the old and make it new, one will at once see the ordinary turned into the sage. I earnestly reflect that the work is not the work of one strength, but must be joined from many strengths; the matter belongs to many people, each planting his own fruit of blessing. A single brick or half a tile is in every case a supreme good cause; a grain of rice or a coin is in every case a bodhi seed. May each only follow his own mind; there is originally no fixed rule. If there be a bold great man, let him too take it on one shoulder. Make the small serve the great; join the short to mend the long. Together accomplish one flavor of ghee and perfect the ocean-assembly of the ten directions. Then you will see the seven-storied wondrous pagoda springing up in mid-air, and the whole body of Many Treasures Buddha entering samādhi upon his seat. Gods and men will rejoice; ghosts and spirits will revere. May it bless the Sage’s life without bound and secure the imperial domain for a billion years. May it at once cause the ancestral meaning that came from the West to be taken up again in the southern sky, and the Chan wind of eastern Yue to be proclaimed again beyond the ranges. May the udumbara blossom appear in three thousand worlds, and the vajra seed be nourished through a hundred million. The merit cannot be reckoned; the blessing and benefit are without end. May the wise early arouse a sincere mind, and hope that the fruit of merit be quickly completed here and now. I reverently hold up this brief memorial and announce it to the ten directions. If one who has the conditions meets it, let him inscribe his fragrant name.
A Memorial for Rebuilding the Halls of the Patriarchal Court at Caoxi

I bow before the truth that the Tathāgata appeared in the world, descending from Tuṣita into the royal palace; and that the Dharma’s unfolding opened its foundation when it came from India to the land of Hua. Beneath the bodhi tree was the place of his attainment of the Way; in the Jetavana grove was the place of his teaching. Spreading gold upon the ground opened the door of generosity; the white horse bearing the scriptures opened the road through the dark night. He opened the good plan of the Three Jewels and set the model of the One Vehicle. Though this be called the ultimate, it is still halfway. Only when the Sugata showed his extinction and his transforming conditions were about to end did he furl the banner he had set up and turn the drum of poisoned coating. Then suddenly he held up the flower and brought forth the essential Way, pointing directly at the very thing before the man, so that he suddenly saw his own mind; he proclaimed the family wind of what lies beyond, and made clear the original nature. Thus Chan arose from this, and the Buddha-dharma became complete thereby. In the Western Heavens twenty-eight patriarchs made the Way of prajñā greatly pervasive; in the Eastern Land the six, beginning with Bodhidharma, first made his lineage illustrious. From Mount Song, where the source was deepened, it branched out at Lingnan. From that time the Way covered the world and its transforming influence soaked the seas, all by the power of the Great Mirror Chan Master, the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi. I revere the Chan Master, whose virtue was endowed by innate knowing and whose Way outshone the sages before him. Far back, Venerable Buddhaśānta left a prophecy, and the bodhi tree was planted in the Song dynasty; Zhiyao sought out the stream, and Baolin Mountain was opened in the Liang. Cao Shuliang imitated the old deed of spreading gold, and the Brahmā-monastery rose; Chen Yaxian gave up his seat as a field of blessing, and the great monastery flourished. Thereupon the Heavenly King sent down a decree on purple clay, and its radiance shone over woods and springs; famous scholars bestowed essays in colored brushes, and their writing hung in bamboo and silk. Chinese and barbarian looked up to the heaven of Tuṣita; dragons and elephants trod the road of practice. Great indeed was that surpassing affair, a ford and bridge through vast kalpas; mighty indeed that heroic model, establishing incense and fire for ten thousand years. Truly a wonder of the world, a surpassing prospect within the realm. From then on the lamp of wisdom shone high, shattering the heavy darkness of the endless night; the Dharma-drum sounded long, waking the great dream of sentient beings. Always those who took refuge came like a market, and those who reverently sacrificed were as to a god. Dynasty after dynasty followed on, a thousand autumns as one day. Yet alas, prosperity and decline have their number, and rise and fall depend on men. The transforming teaching gradually waned; the conditions of the Way little by little decayed. The community of monks met with demonic obstruction and their pure cultivation was ruined; the halls and buildings were battered by wind and rain and their magnificence fell. The bases of the pillars rotted, the beams and ridgepoles leaned and tilted. I sigh over the great house about to topple — it is not something one beam can hold up; and I lament the good conditions not yet joined — they must rely on many people to be accomplished. We monks of the temple, born into a flourishing age and entering the empty gate early, shelter on this famous mountain and unworthily inherit the last descendants. Morning and evening we attend and revere, serving the true images as in those years; at dusk the drum and at dawn the bell, we continue the incense and fire in these late days. Truly we see the living dragon and white elephant, and the atmosphere is as it was; and we grieve over these broken tiles and ruined rafters, the halls and shrines collapsed and destroyed. They let the Great Beings drink the pestilential mists of the smoking hills, and the Tathāgata wear clothing of mist and dew. The mountain’s hues veil his pure body; the birds’ voices speak his endless verses. Green moss covers the long corridors — how is this the adornment of a Buddha-land? Gray rats scurry over the ancient tiles — hardly can it be called a way-place of ultimate bliss. The realm, though it be true in every matter, is made common by men even where it is true. If one does not urgently repair the house, I fear it will collapse in a moment. If one can remove the old and make it new, one will at once see the ordinary turned into the sage. Therefore I arouse a great vow and set in motion a vast mind: to reopen the treasure-ground in particular and renew the Buddha-sun in mid-heaven, hoping to turn the Dharma-wheel once more and drive the ship of compassion on the sea of suffering. Therefore I have respectfully chosen the full-moon day of the tenth month of the twenty-sixth year to first open the surpassing Avataṃsaka assembly, selecting fifty-three monks of pure precepts to sit a thousand-day long term; and next to transform the famous lords of the present age to repair twelve halls and shrines. May it bless ten thousand years of the Sage’s life, so that every place is a way-place, and may every person accomplish the fruit of Buddhahood. I reflect that extraordinary matters must await extraordinary men, and that world-rare merit must have world-rare wisdom. Therefore I reverently hold up this brief memorial and announce it to all great donors: cultivate together the pure cause and jointly bind the fruit of bodhi. Yet since the Dharma has no fixed marks and its spreading depends on men, and wealth is not measured by amount and the giving lies with oneself. I have heard that a single drop of water is no different in its moistening nature from the ocean’s vastness, and that the space within a mustard-seed’s hollow is no other than the vastness of the great void. One who is free of marks has blessing beyond thought; one who clings to traces has merit that is not vast. If one joyfully arouses the mind, one will at once see a Buddha-land of treasure-kings appear at the tip of a single hair; and if one clears the throat and snaps the fingers, one can straightway turn the great Dharma-wheel within a single mote of dust. Thus Caoxi, dried up, will swell again; the lamp of wisdom, dimmed, will shine again; the udumbara blossom will appear in three thousand worlds; the seed of prajñā will be nourished through a hundred million; Baolin will double its worth over former days, and Vulture Peak will be renewed on this day. For those who aid and support, blessing and long life will equal the high and the deep; for those who protect and uphold, merit will be as lasting as river and hill. Spread the imperial wind to the eight bounds; sprinkle sweet dew upon the ten directions. Those who see and hear and rejoice will all ascend to the land of benevolence and long life; those who revere, invoke and take refuge will together reach the shore of bodhi. The vow being thus vast, the blessing is without bound. Looking up in hope of your benevolence, may all respond in one voice. I reverently set forth this memorial.
A Memorial for Repairing the Portrait Hall of the Five Patriarchs at Caoxi

At the Baolin way-place of Nanhua Chan Temple the true body of the Sixth Patriarch is present, and the robe and bowl of Bodhidharma remain. From the Second Patriarch down to Huangmei, the transmission of five generations ends here; from the Tang down to this day, one stream of water has flowed on. Therefore a hall of the Five Patriarchs has been established to express the succession of transmission and reception. Now that years have passed and long ages gone, it has bitterly suffered the ravages of wind and rain; as months transform and days pass, at once the bases of the pillars are seen to rot. If one does not seize the time and rescue it urgently, I truly fear it cannot be held up another day. If one can remove the old and make it new, it will at once shine and dazzle the eye. The adorned towers and pavilions will spring up before your eyes; the whole bodies of the Five Patriarchs will enter samādhi upon their seats. Gods and men will rejoice; ghosts and spirits will revere. May it bless the Sage’s life without bound and secure the imperial domain forever firm. The merit cannot be reckoned; the blessing and benefit are without end. May the wise arouse a sincere mind early, and hope that the fruit of merit be quickly completed here and now.
A Memorial for Copying the Avataṃsaka Sutra and Receiving the Ten Directions

Not moving a single step while the mind pervades the ten directions is called “sitting in participation.” Not rising from the cessation-samādhi while manifesting all deportments is called “wondrous practice.” This lies in the man’s own faith; there is no need to seek it by galloping outward. I have heard with reverence that the great Avataṃsaka Sutra is the fundamental Dharma-wheel of Vairocana, and that the ancient temple of Caoxi is the true lineage of the Sixth Patriarch’s Chan. The Dharma-realm is the mysterious capital of all sages; the monastery is the home to which the ten directions return. From ancient times to now, eminent wanderers of the clouds and water who came to revere the Patriarch have been present at every hour; yet for a whole year and to the end of the year, food and drink and quiet dwelling given according to each person — of this there has never been any at all. I, an old and worn man, since coming to this mountain, have from the first kept this in mind; outside the mountain gate I have set up one Hall of the Ten Directions to receive those who come from the four quarters, and all that is needed for food and drink comes from the permanent abode of the Chan hall. Yet alas, from the beginning those in charge have not been the right men: the common rabble has gathered in confusion and turned it into a place of filth. Not only did this betray my original mind, it also wasted the faithful’s offerings to no purpose. Now my disciple Mingzhong has aroused a vast mind and practices the conduct of Samantabhadra. He vows to dwell in this hall and write out one copy of the honored Avataṃsaka Sutra, and by this Dharma-grace to gather in body and mind — and thereby to receive the worthy and holy of the ten directions. When I, the old and worn man, heard this, I praised it and rejoiced, and said to him: “Long ago the youth Sudhana visited fifty-three good teachers and still traveled through a hundred cities. Now you, without moving half a step, revere all the worthy and holy who come from the ten directions of the world. This may be called the most surpassing merit. How fortunate to be born in this Dharma-ending age, to dwell in such a way-place, to write such a great Dharma, to cultivate such wondrous practice, to accumulate such a surpassing cause. It may be called offering this body and mind to the dust-motes of worlds — and that is what is meant by repaying the Buddha’s grace.” What I pray is that those who see and hear and rejoice may have blessing equal to the sands of the Ganges, and those who aid and praise may have merit beyond vast kalpas; how much more those who give the seven treasures to make adornment and provide the four requisites as offerings — their blessing again cannot be thought or discussed.
A Memorial for Building a Tea-Offering Hut at Kuteng Ridge in Dianbai County, Gaozhou

I bow before the truth that on the road of gods and men, making blessing comes first; and that on the journey of birth and death, relieving others is the first thing. I have heard that the gates of a marquis’s house are like the sea: they love the rich but do not respect the poor. The Way of the sages is like Heaven: it succors the urgent but does not add to the rich. Therefore the hungry are easily fed, and so a single meal has drawn a reward of a thousand gold; the thirsty are easily given drink, and so a bowl of broth has brought the repayment of one who pushed the cart. These are but the affairs of sentient beings, and even so the repayment comes thus; how much more the unconditioned field of blessing, whose merit cannot be thought or discussed? Now, north of Gaozhou and south of Shendian, high mountains pierce the Milky Way and steep ridges bar the sky. This is the throat of the seas beyond and the gate of Luopang. In former years travelers’ carts could not pass side by side; today how could the footsteps of traders go alone? Truly it is a fearful road of fame and profit, truly a lair of robbers and thieves. It relied on the years after Jiajing and Longqing, after the royal army broke the bandits, to change the perilous road into a level road and turn stubborn customs toward the imperial wind. Though coming and going still has the toil of trudging, advance and halt are no longer guarded against wolves. But being a burning region on red frontiers, with pestilent miasmas and mountain mists, and with poisonous vapors steaming and hot springs rolling, travelers at the world’s end are like men treading fire and entering boiling water; soldiers on distant garrison are like men who have missed the burning and step into a cauldron. Shoulder to shoulder and heel to heel, they gather their sleeves and make a cloud; climbing peaks and clutching at woods, they truly drip sweat like rain. Lips dry and tongue parched, they long for a spoonful of water as a great drought longs for cloud and rainbow; throat aflame and bowels scorched, they find a drop like one parched with thirst drinking sweet dew. Moreover, a hundred li to one post-house, a whole day to half a meal. Servants sweat blood, carts and horses are soaked through; they raise their eyes and see no kin, and this suffering has none to tell. All this is the craving for fame and the chase of profit, seeing gain and forgetting form. They know only how to pick up earth and make gold; who understands throwing a brick to draw jade? Moreover, the lowly of the frontier and the mlecchas: their customs love ghosts and honor licentious shrines; the people take life lightly and delight in killing and stealing. Though it be a foot of cloth or a peck of millet, they seize it from others wrongfully; how then would they gladly give a grain of rice or a coin themselves? Thus their bodhi seeds turn ever more scorched and withered, and the sprouts of their good roots daily rot. Therefore the wicked grow wickeder and the poor grow poorer; delusion piles on delusion, and the more they are taught the harder they are to teach. Lately we have been fortunate to meet the great officials of the way, who widely love and bestow benevolence, relieving men and benefiting beings, awakening the people by this Way and continuing the sages of the past while opening the learning to come. They found stupas in the prefectures and counties and raise the most surpassing Dharma-banner; they set up the red flag at Jetavana and do the inconceivable Buddha-work. These may be called ships of the world’s age and precious caskets for the ford of delusion. I, a mountain monk, because I spread the Dharma, met with calamity, and by grace was banished to Leiyang. Cast into the far wilds ten thousand li away, I bore arms at Dianbai. Climbing the ridge of Bitter Vine, thirsting on the high plain, I thought of the sweet dew’s juice; wandering back and forth on the perilous road, I happened to see two monks who had built a hut beside the way. I held up one bowl of fragrant tea in fullest respect at the horse’s head. Someone received it gladly with tears, and in sorrow was moved to grief. Who would have thought that in a land of pestilence I would chance upon companions of Tiantai? Resting a little at leisure in the woods, I then carved an inscription on the stone, and from this I aroused a vow: that in this place I would build a great vihāra, and would use the matter at hand to make the mind clear and the tea to proclaim the Dharma. From then the years rolled on, and two years passed in a flash. Then in the summer of the wuxu year I met Magistrate Wan of Gaozhou, by chance in the city of the immortal ram, and we talked of the thread of Vulture Peak. When I spoke of this, he greatly marveled, saying, “How strange!” So I begged him to be a bridge and ford for the Dharma and ventured to ask him to be a compassionate donor, hoping to rebuild this phantom city and lead the many back to the treasure-land. And I wished to turn this defiled land into a Pure Land, exchanging tiles and stones for thatch; though it need not be glorious with gold and jasper, it should still provide both Dharma and food. But I reflect that the work is not the work of one strength and must be bound by conditions with many people. Therefore I reverently compose this brief memorial and announce it to the ten directions, entrusting it to good men so-and-so to bow their heads before noble officials, greet elders, traders and travelers, scholars and officials and eminent men. I humbly pray that you arouse a vast mind and form the thought of what is hard to meet. Moreover, every person is a Buddha: you need only consent and take it up yourself. Every dharma is true: what thing is not giving? Be it much or little, coarse or fine, falling dew can swell a stream, and light dust can complete a mountain. Though for a time three carts are set outside the gate and names are borrowed to lead them on, to let them pass straight through to the road that goes beyond is truly compassion. If one can only break open the purse of stinginess, one will at once see the adorned Buddha-land. For those who pass by, coming and going, let them be offered a single bowl: in Old Zhao’s cup shall float the gleaming white snow. For the thirsty to drink and the hungry to eat, let them force down seven bowls: beneath Lu Tong’s arms shall rise the gentle, whistling clear breeze. It dispels fevered affliction and brings coolness, dissolves fatigue and scatters drowsiness. With the water of Dharma it irrigates the seeds of bodhi and increases the numinous sprouts; with good roots it plants the field of prajñā and can accomplish the holy fruit. From this the breast becomes free and unconstrained, and going or staying is easy and untroubled. It may be called a way-place of ultimate bliss, named a joyful Buddha-work. Spread the vastness of the compassionate wind and sweep away all the miasmic mist of the pestilent sea; hang up the perfect brightness of the Buddha-sun and shatter the illusory dream of the dark road. May the icchantikas do away with the perversity of killing, stealing and lust; may the mlecchas not fall into the ghost-realm of rākṣasas. One man good and many good, goodness filling the frontier land; one family at peace and all families at peace, peace securing the seas and the world. Together ascend to the land of benevolence and long life and behold together the transforming rule of brightness and joy. By this merit may the Sage’s life be blessed without bound, and with this body and mind may the ruler’s grace be repaid though it be boundless. The blessing is not set in vain; how could the matter be idle talk? May you only approve and aid it, and spare no lingering. I reverently set forth this memorial. Written at dawn of the mid-autumn month of the wuxu year of Wanli, in the Traveler’s Rest Studio of the Immortal City.
A Memorial for Rebuilding the Puji Temple at Taiping Bridge in Nanxiong Prefecture

I bow before the truth that this famous region beyond the ranges is a single thread drawing the life-vein of Chinese and barbarian; and that the ancient crossing of Taiping is a flying rainbow locking the throat of a hundred Yue. Merchants from within the realm — how could any of them not pass this way? Rare treasures from beyond the seas must all come through here. How sad that at this crowded ford of vast kalpas, who can rely on the precious raft? On the wild waves of the sea of suffering, the compassionate ship can ferry one across. I revere the Puji Temple by the Taiping bridge: it established its rule in former ages, its affairs looking up to earlier worthies. Facing the Ling River, it is like the Ganges at Śrāvastī; backed by Meikui, it is as the Jetavana of Kapilavastu. It grips the source of the South Sea and holds the surpassing prospect of the mighty pass. Truly a ford and bridge through all ages, truly a safe crossing of the long road. But as days come and months go, rain thins and wind wears; the age changes and time shifts, the beams break and the ridgepoles rot. Illusory blossoms easily fade; the sun’s shimmer cannot be kept. They have shut up the Three Jewels so that they are not manifest, and the minds of the many return with nowhere to rest. Now we are fortunate to meet a benevolent man in office who wishes to remove the old and make it new, and gentlemen who keep it in mind, who will rescue what has gone astray and mend what is broken. I, a mountain monk, venture to take up the wooden bell and raise my voice; may the worthy and eminent among scholars and commoners catch the wind and echo it. It is only that human nature is all good and must wait to be moved before it penetrates. Yet though the Buddha’s teaching has its conditions, how could it not respond without being sought? Therefore I reverently hold up this brief memorial and announce it to the ten directions. I humbly hope that the rich and noble will exert their strength to repay the grace of former lives, and the poor and lowly will contribute their labor, hoping to plant the fruit of lives to come. May only this be: where the purse of stinginess is broken, the vajra seed reveals its radiance; when the water of craving dries up, the ship of prajñā reaches the other shore. Be it passers-by or traders, every bodhi seed will perfectly ripen and every person may reach the land of ultimate bliss. Say not that the blessing equals the sands of the Ganges; rather rejoice that the mind returns to the treasure-land. The merit surpasses the conditioned; the virtue bears without bound. May it bless the Sage’s life as lasting as rivers and mountains and spread its flowing light as long as sun and moon. May all under the falling frost and dew alike submit to the compassionate wind, and wherever cart and boat can reach, all look up with reverence to the sun of wisdom. Such benefit cannot be exhausted in praise. Please inscribe your fragrant name, hoping to leave it imperishable.
A Memorial for Rebuilding Jetavana Temple

I bow before the truth that in the worlds of the ten directions every place is a way-place, and one who has the eye can see it; and that the eighty thousand dusts of toil are in every case nothing but Buddha-work, and one who understands the mind knows it himself. Moreover there is the model of spreading gold, which we follow as the family wind of the ancient Buddhas; and I have pondered the excellent plan of leaving a belt, which is precisely the rule for officials. Only, affairs follow opportunity and the Way spreads by men; the season is hard to meet and good conditions join by chance. Now the ancient monastery of Jetavana was founded in the Tang dynasty, as the records plainly show, and was revered with rites and offerings. I regret that the mountain spirit did not keep it, and it suddenly fell into brambles; but relying on the knowing protection of Dharma-guardians, the thicket of thorns was suddenly opened. Formerly it met with sons of the five heinous deeds, and the Buddha and Patriarchs had almost nowhere to rely on; now it relies on the three feet of Heaven, and gods and men are fortunate to have a support. Yet the halls and shrines lean and fall; the golden images are chill in wind and rain. Incense and lamps are extinguished, and the Brahmā-voice is silent morning and dusk. I, the mountain monk Rujian, happened to come begging for food and hung my staff at Lingjiang, opening a pure dwelling on the Ganges and spreading out a bamboo grove by the outer wall. But I fear the great house cannot be completed by one beam; it must rely on lofty worthies, and with the strength of many it is easily raised. To pick up an inch of grass and make it a Brahmā-monastery is of itself the Heavenly Emperor’s hammer and forge; to split open a mote of dust and bring forth the scriptures could only be Samantabhadra’s device. I humbly hope that you will all put forth hand and eye, each wagering his spiritual power, gathering the small into much and from small reaching great. Let ghosts and spirits haul and transport, not yielding to Mount Sumeru; and at once see gold and jasper shine together, becoming a Pure Land outright. The transformation follows the mind; the enjoyment is in oneself. Take the repayment as the proof of this, and may the merit be imperishable together.
A Memorial for Rebuilding the Tower of Universal Vows for Liberating Life and Accomplishing Buddhahood at Huxin Temple

The Buddha’s great compassion delivers all alike through the ten directions, so that every sentient being in the whole Dharma-realm may all become Buddhas. Hence it is said, “So long as one sentient being has not become a Buddha, I vow not to take bodhi.” This is the Buddha’s vow to deliver beings. The Prajñā says, “He delivered innumerable, countless, boundless sentient beings all into extinction, and in truth there is not one sentient being who attained extinction.” This is the actual proof that sentient beings become Buddhas. Through the ages those who cultivate and vow to become Buddhas are many, but those who now deliver boundless sentient beings are few; for each forms the thought that after becoming a Buddha he will then deliver beings, not knowing that right now, in the present, one who can deliver beings with a Buddha’s mind is practicing the true wondrous conduct of Buddhahood. Of the practices that broadly deliver beings, none surpasses the single gate of liberating life. Formerly there were the Great Master Tiantai, and next the Great Master Yongming, who when he was an official used his salary to buy living creatures and set them free, and thereby did not die; this is something everyone knows today. From then to now, only Great Master Yunqi has been able to imitate the conduct of these two masters. West Lake was anciently a pond for liberating life; now only the Three Pools have been dredged, and a causeway built to make a pond, taking but a fraction of it. Moreover West Lake has from of old been a place of song and dance, in truth a place of lakes of wine and forests of meat. Now in the lake there are these three ponds, and the creatures released in them fill them full: this is a transformation, within the sea of karma, into a Buddha-land of ultimate bliss. Yet the painted barges with their songs and dances that pass by these ponds never once turn back to look: they are still in drunken dream. One mind makes purity or defilement, and suffering or joy depends on it. How far apart are “yes” and “aye”? In this pond there is Huxin Temple, and the temple has three towers. The temple has been rebuilt, but the towers are not yet made, and the causeway cannot yet keep out the water. I rejoiced at the pond and praised the compassion of Dharma Master Xuanjin, and lamented that his work had not reached completion — I felt great regret. Returning, I lay down at night and dreamed I walked on the causeway; the sand underfoot had, grain by grain, a Buddha’s name on every face, and those who followed me did not dare set foot. I said, “You know that the whole earth is Buddha and there is no place to put your foot down; this is precisely the time of your practice.” So I told the assembly, “If we gather this sand into a Buddha-tower, then the givers and what is given will together ascend to the Pure Land of ultimate bliss.” Waking, I thought of it and thereupon aroused the thought of universal deliverance, praying that the creatures released there may escape suffering and become Buddhas. And those crawling things — I look on them as Buddhas; how much more these living people now, the most numinous and most bright: how could one look on them as mere sentient beings? Why not vow that the sentient beings easy to deliver before our eyes be first made the object of the thought of Buddhahood, and with many vows deliver those many sentient beings?
