In this way not only is what is delivered more vast; by joining many minds to guard this pond, the guarding is the firmer. Is such conduct and vow not the contemplation in which mind, Buddha and sentient beings are equal without difference? Therefore I devise a plan for universal transformation: each person gives ten coins and recites the Buddha’s name a hundred times; joining many minds in one Buddha, gathering many people to make three towers. What is given is small, what is accomplished is great; this is the sea of accumulated blessing and merit. And this delivers as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand by as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand — a power even greater; is it not the most surpassing Buddha-work? If it arises from this, and in time the whole lake becomes a lotus pond, then the sentient beings of this region, rich and poor, noble and base alike, will all together be born in the Buddha-land of ultimate bliss. Is that not wondrous conduct?
A Memorial for Rebuilding Longhua Temple

The hills and waters of old Hangzhou are numinous and lovely; in the Song dynasty temples were founded there like stars, their bells and drums within hearing of one another. Longhua stands southwest of Nanping. It was founded by the Great Scholar Fu of the Liang dynasty, more than a thousand years ago. Sima Wengong once had a shrine here; now all is abandoned. Its ground not only holds the beauty of hills and waters but is the key junction between Putuo and Tiantai, a place the wanderers of the ten directions must pass. In Qiantang the temple banners face one another, yet a place where a pilgrim may rest his shoulder is not easy to find. Formerly the monk Sankong of Funiu came and was moved to pity; the layman Hong Yunquan of Jianggan invited him here. The foundation was not yet complete, and yet those who gathered were always full; after a short stay he soon departed. The Chan monk Guangkun aroused a vast mind, vowing to build it into a way-place of reception. In the spring of the yisi year I happened to pass this way and saw the Buddha images wondrously adorned, and was born again into thirsting admiration. Pacing about and observing the configuration, backed by the imperial stockade and facing Qiantang, it is the most surpassing of places. When the wanderers of the ten directions reach here they are at the very point of exhausted strength and wearied spirit, seeking a moment’s rest and unable to find it. If they can find a place to set foot and rest the body, and a drop of water to touch the lips, it is like pouring ghee and drinking sweet dew: this binds the most surpassing condition of merit. And I saw the Chan man’s compassion, earnest and deep, and the good men who for a time aroused the mind, each leaping with joy: this is the most surpassing cause. But the work of the temple is great and its cost huge, the days and months long and the people many; unless there be a vast donor to do the inconceivable Buddha-work, it will not be easy to fulfill the Chan man’s original vow. I was moved and praised and looked up to him, and made this exposition for him. All officials, elders and laymen, good men and women: if you can truly arouse the rare mind and form the thought of what is hard to meet, cutting open the purse of stinginess and adorning the Buddha-land, then with impermanent wealth you make imperishable work; and if you give your body and surrender your house, dragon spirits will guard it and it will not cease through ten thousand generations. Compared with the works of the dusty world — a thousand years of fields with eight hundred owners — what a difference as between Heaven and earth! Moreover, making the causes and conditions of a Pure Land and the Buddha-seed of lives to come, may you hope, when Maitreya descends, to be foremost among the kin at the three assemblies of Longhua. Is that not the first and most surpassing merit of the world beyond? Because every person has the Buddha-nature and each is endowed with a former cause, surely you will see today’s condition and not be willing to let it pass you by. How could you bear to return empty-handed from the mountain of treasures? This lies with all of you who have wisdom: at once arouse measureless joy and quickly put forth the strength of the bold.
The Vow for Writing Out the Avataṃsaka Sutra in Blood and Gold

I bow to the all-pervading Dharma-realm, to the ten directions and the three times, to the lotus flower’s wondrous adornment, to the pure mote-of-dust lands, to the Great Enlightened Supreme Honored One, whose division-bodies fill everywhere, who proclaims the pure ocean of the sūtras’ definitive meaning of nature and marks, free of all marks of letters, in the seven places and nine assemblies, together with Mañjuśrī and all great beings, the good teachers countless as motes of dust, and the pure assembly of worthy monks. I now spread the three karmas and revere the ultimate emptiness; only with the unconditioned compassion that illumines my true vow. Mindful that from beginningless time I have wandered through birth and death, turning and turning in the realms of suffering, like a great fire-wheel, casting off bodies and receiving bodies in inconceivable numbers, and all the evil karma I have done — the Buddha alone knows and sees it. Now relying on the power of the Three Jewels, I have come among men and my six faculties are whole; but my mind and consciousness are much darkened. By the slight good roots of past lives I left early the sea of love and affection, yet still I entered the dense forest of the common, like one fleeing drowning and leaping into fire. Within, borrowing the fumigation of good strength, mind after mind vows to leave far away; without, gaining the moistening of the Dharma-rain, a pure sprout suddenly grows. But because the dust of habit blazes, at times it is seen to dry up again. Excellent indeed are the great good friends who are to me as a heaven-sent gift; by this great cause and condition I have escaped the fevered affliction and together return to the realm of coolness, to behold and revere the Honored Mañjuśrī and delight to dwell in an aranya, the deepest and stillest place. But the mind’s thought is like a monkey, and one sees ever more the marks of grasping; the power of prajñā is faint and weak, and hard to match the army of birth and death. For this cause, seeing the practice of all practices, I bow to the Lotus Treasury, the perfect and wondrous Supreme Vehicle, and vow to arouse the mind of reverent refuge, and to receive and uphold it with my whole life, bowing my head. I have heard that of the bodhisattva conduct of Samantabhadra, vast and inconceivable, among the six ways of receiving and upholding, writing out is the first. With a bone pen and blood for ink, through kalpas numerous as motes of dust, one accumulates such sūtras until their measure equals a thousand worlds. I have heard such a vow, hard to equal. I will take only blood for ink, mingled together with gold, and write out the great sūtra’s single characters, the ocean of Dharma-gates. By this surpassing cause, may it be a boat and oar on the sea of suffering. May every drop of this body’s blood of mine accord with the Dharma-nature and melt into the ocean of the Lotus Treasury, moistening the realms of sentient beings everywhere. As I hold the brush and write with my hand, may point and stroke make the mind free; and may this illusory body of mine forever gain the vajra body. May the body be like Mount Purple Gold, dignified and grave beyond all compare, so that hearing the name and seeing the form bring great joy to the mind. May the hands be like a great treasure-mound, ever bringing forth the wealth of the world, the seven treasures and the four requisites, all things filled full. Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, may all sentient beings, poor and sick, obtain all they seek as they wish. When I become a Buddha, may my land be utterly pure, with only beings of the Supreme Vehicle and none of the sufferings of evil paths, and may I ever proclaim this Dharma-wheel to the utmost of kalpas numerous as motes. I was born in the Dharma-ending age, my power of faith slight, ever accompanied by the lid of delusion, and hard put to escape the karma of birth and death. My good roots are not yet ripe; if I fall into the wheel of rebirth, may this surpassing cause keep me from falling into evil destinies, and may I ever be born in pure Buddha-lands, never apart from the Three Jewels, and early awaken to the emptiness of self-nature and leap beyond all that is outflows. In all that I do, may I forever be free of the obstruction of the three poisons. I uphold this by the power of vow until the end of the future. May these sūtra scrolls of mine not be destroyed by the three calamities. When Maitreya is about to descend, may light shine forth from these sūtras and illumine the worlds of the ten directions, with the six great quakings. When Maitreya has descended and first sits beneath the Longhua tree, may these sūtras emerge from the earth and leap up in the midst of space, each character giving forth a wondrous sound declaring the vow I originally made. May the millions of gods and men all call it a rare thing; and may I then be in that assembly, expounding the true meaning. Whenever a Buddha appears in the world, in the first twenty-one days he proclaims the great Avataṃsaka; may I be first among the fitting vessels. Though this body of mine is illusory and false, born of father and mother, yet relying on this false root I accomplish the true matter. May my father be like pure Brahmā and my mother like Lady Māyā; when the Buddhas descend, may they be born through my father and mother. My teacher has delivered me; the grace of Dharma is the most honored. May I be a guiding teacher in the assemblies of all Buddhas. My friends are most sincere and true, lifting me up to walk the right path; may my friends be like Mañjuśrī, the first of good teachers. May the great faith of donors and their vast giving of wealth and goods — may all these wise people forever escape the suffering of stinginess and craving. When the Buddhas appear in the world and first are asked to teach, may they spare neither body, life nor wealth but broadly cultivate all good karma. As I practice thus, relying on all who uphold it, may all these worthy and holy ones never be apart from me life after life; in whatever Buddha-land, may we together raise up the Buddha-dharma. And all who see and hear, who praise and proclaim, every slightest good cause and condition — may all return to the ocean of the Lotus Treasury. I arouse such a vow, vast beyond exhaustion, to the very end of the future, until the mind is perfectly complete.
An Essay on Liberating Life

Living beings live of themselves — why liberate them? And why make liberating life a Buddha-work? Pei Xiu said, “Whatever has blood and breath must have awareness, and whatever has awareness must share one body.” Hence it is said, “Even crawling things that contain a spirit all have the Buddha-nature.” Since the nature is Buddha, to kill a living being is to kill a Buddha; and it is not only that: one who kills living beings has no compassionate mind, and so cuts off the Buddha-seed nature. Those crawling creatures men think may be killed — they do not know that their own originally possessed, luminous Buddha-nature — how could it be cut off? The mind that does not kill is the compassionate mind. Compassion is called benevolence; pity is the inability to bear. The mind that cannot bear is the beginning of benevolence. Hence seeing the living, one cannot bear to see them die; hearing their cries, one cannot bear to eat their flesh. This was first proclaimed by the sages and worthies — how could it be the Buddhists alone? The Confucians, because of their station, merely keep the kitchen at a distance; the Buddha, because he practices compassion equally, extends it to all. Yet among those who liberate life there is the difference between clinging to marks and forgetting marks, and those who imitate it do not escape the abuse of liberating life turning into killing life. Therefore the Dharma values forgetting marks, and the wonder lies in following conditions; the root is dwelling in nothing, and the fault is the taint of outflows. If one can meet conditions and make them the root, then wherever the eye falls there is life, and wherever one arrives there is Buddha-work. Every thing and every instance is a gate of joyful giving; every thought and every mind is a realm of compassion. Why then must one be bound to assemblies and covenants, clinging to merit, or set fixed terms and strictly enforce rules? The Chan man Ming has long cherished this vow; if he carries it out, compassion will spread daily wider and the realm transformed will daily grow broader. Uphold it for ten years, and there will surely be measureless youths making offerings — what doubt is there?
A Sacrificial Address for Lu, Grand Administrator, the Layman of Mount Wutai

Alas! You received the secret charge at Vulture Peak and came into this turbid world to benefit beings. Your coming was no coming; therefore you did not reveal your original countenance. And your going is no going; you left only an iron heart. For more than eighty years you played your part on the stage, and your wondrous virtue, vast as the sands of the Ganges, took every Buddha as its root. You served your ruler with a Buddha’s mind, and your ruler alone was Buddha to you; you loved things with a true mind, and things alone were true. Hence the matter that lay beyond, all your life, never left the edge of your official cap; and the final word at your departure you entrusted to your sons and daughters. In you appeared the body of an official that is no official’s body; in me, to my shame, the marks of a bhikṣu that are no bhikṣu’s marks. Yet though our roads differ, in truth we keep house in the same way. I am grateful that, at the moment of your setting out but not yet setting out, you sent half a sheet of paper as a letter to Lingnan, bidding me, amid emptiness and non-emptiness, draw a drop of Caoxi’s water and make it an offering of sweet dew, to present to the Honored One of the Abhiṣeka. Alas! The level lake and the full moon behold the pure Dharma-body; heavenly music fills the sky and gives forth the vast and long tongue. Receive this savor of Dharma and thereby mirror this heart of the bramble. May you enjoy the offering.
A Sacrificial Address for Hu, Grand Censor, the Master Shun’an

Alas, how it pains me! Are you alive, sir, or dead? I have sought it over and over and cannot find the reason. When word of your death suddenly came, they said you were dead; yet when I read your poem written as you changed mats, you plainly told men that you were not dead, and men did not understand. Only I plainly know that you are not dead, and I speak it, fearing only that men will not believe me. Alas, how sad! Think how you and I met by chance in the midst of the great transformation, and for more than thirty years it was as one day — surely this is strange. At first I met you in the wilds of Shouyang; at one glance our minds were at odds with nothing. I abruptly spoke to you of the one calamity and blessing, of making life and death equal, and you were already glad at heart and found it fitting. Afterward you sought me again on the cool mountain, and we sat cross-legged beneath a cliff a thousand feet of cold and laughed and talked amid the snows of ten thousand years, chewing hard ice and eating coarse rice, a vast kalpa in a single breath. Then you already had the thought of climbing heaven and grasping the mist, the aspiration to rise far beyond. Yet I did not know it was hidden. Not long after, I visited you at Yanmen and sat in your tent as though in an empty valley; we joined our beds and shared our covers, and for three months we were never apart, day and night giving forth our thoughts. Then you were already clear, silently tallying in your mind. From this I knew that you looked on carriage and crown as dust and grime, and on body and world as the wing of a cicada. So we made a tryst on the Eastern Sea, to eat the morning rainbow and build a tower to dwell in. Afterward you indeed released me from the dust’s yoke, and I, for your sake, forgot going and staying. At that time I played with you in the light of the ocean-seal: a long wave of ten thousand li, bright and wholly blue, as though we stood before a jeweled mirror and trod on lapis lazuli, sat on a lotus and dwelt in a Pure Land, not knowing that this body was in Heaven and Earth, or that outer things were in this body; and our joy had not yet reached its end. Suddenly the Heavenly Emperor was angry that I had lightly bored open Chaos, scattered simplicity and diluted the pure, and punished me with nine deaths, banishing me to the land of pestilence. Then I took my everlasting leave of you. You thought I would surely die, and would have sent a lament to summon me back. Then ten years passed like a single breath, and at every moment I knew you were thinking of me and binding your thoughts in the cold clouds, weeping for me and piling up tears like a long river; and you did not know that I was roaming with you as in former days, plainly before your brows and lashes, with no gap of a hair between waking and sleeping. Alas, how sad! In the fifth month of that year you sent a foot of fine silk to comfort me ten thousand li away; I sent an attendant to inquire after you in the seventh month. I took pleasure in a poem of yours that I cherished, saying it was “most like Vimalakīrti’s body in illness.” The letter arrived, and you had already shown your sickness. You held my letter and recited my poem while you were still able to speak, and a month later you passed away. So I comforted you with my whole life, and you took your leave of me as though face to face: this too is strange. When I formerly took leave of you, it was not like your taking leave of me now. That I should think of you and weep for you — is it not like your thinking of me and weeping for me? Your birth was no chance. You bore a lofty and enlightened view and embraced a talent not of this age; your loyalty was to the altar of soil and grain, your heart was with the common people. Your years had an end, but your talent had not; your form changed, but your mind does not change. As your deathbed poem says, “The numinous root ever attends the brightness of the moon.” Seen thus, you looked on death and life as night and dawn, a thousand ages as one day. Your spirit roams the vast desert, hearing the music of Heaven and dwelling in the broad palace, companion to flying immortals and of endless life. You look on former days as dung and soil. Who knows that your joy now is surpassingly greater than in former times? Since you are joyful, why should I grieve? Alas, how sorrowful! May you enjoy the offering.
A Sacrificial Address for Great Master Daguan

In the forty-fourth year of Wanli, the year being bingchen, on the first day of the eleventh month, gengzi, and on the nineteenth day thereafter, bingxu, I, the former Haiyin śramaṇa Deqing, though unworthy of the teaching, reverently set out an offering of fragrant viands and make sacrifice to the spirit of the Venerable Zibo, Great Master Daguan, saying: Alas! Your birth was no birth: you came riding the power of vow. Your death is no death: you departed in accord with liberation. Coming and going do not fall within common feeling; how could birth and death be the same as worldly truth? As for your dwelling in the world, you held a vajra mind and sat on firm ground. For more than thirty years your daily fare was plain tea and rice, your backbone was pure steel; the seventeen hundred koans were stale rattan, the residue of your nose’s mucus. You pushed over Maitreya and Śākyamuni and did not defer to Deshan and Linji. To others you showed compassion to the utmost; at the moment of meeting you had not the least scruple. You vowed to protect the Dharma as though cherishing your own eyes; you sought the great matter as one who has lost father and mother. Not to be in harmony with worldly feeling — that was your true conduct. You sat at ease in the light of the water-moon and walked alone in the shadows of empty flowers. When first you visited me on the Eastern Sea, you at once cast off bodily form; when we met again on the Western Hills, you searched me to the marrow. When my calamity had not yet taken shape, you told me all its hidden details; and when my trouble had already broken out, you would have washed it away for me. You would have repaid our old tryst at Caoxi and would have knocked at the palace gate in the imperial capital. Braving the scorching heat on the road, you advanced and halted by rumor and echo. You devised many means, hoping to bring me out of nine deaths. Alas! In your service of the Dharma-gate you truly bore the heart of Cheng Ying and Chu Jiu; in your being my true friend you were hardly to be compared with Guan and Bao, Chen and Lei. I was graced by the emperor’s light punishment, yet in your mind it was not yet over. I was banished beyond the ranges, and you waited for me by the river’s isle. At our one meeting sorrow and joy mingled, as though the nine springs had risen again. When you and I took our everlasting leave, I was willing to be a vengeful ghost in the burning region; you charged me to keep my resolve at peace, hoping the dark door would open again. I wiped away my tears and came to the long road; you held my hand and swallowed your grief and did not speak. Then, when we parted at the passes and mountains, the days and months flew like arrows. I knew in my heart that you would not forget me, and you ever urged me not to give up. Holding to the power of your vow, you swore not to betray your original beginning. So you withdrew the flame of the great sword and would not let it be loosed upon the dust; hoping the jade of He would surely be believed, you did not grudge the Sui pearl lightly dashed. You would knock at the ruler’s gate ninefold, when suddenly the whirlwind rose on all four sides. Land and sea surged with waves, dragons and serpents were scattered, jade and stone burned together, and the Dharma-banner toppled. You climbed the broad highway of the eight paths, when suddenly you met the long serpent and the great boar. Heaven truly mirrored your inmost heart, but you saw only the insolence of the petty and vulgar. Fortunately this heart was once made clear, and thereby the depths were brought out. You were truly vast and untroubled — what grief, what joy? Adversity and compliance you took as they came, death and life as a game. Why did former debts seek you out? Truly it was the former condition that made it so. You grieved that the five turbidities could not be borne, and that only a single course of conduct could be relied on. So you rinsed your mouth and sat cross-legged, and thus in stillness you departed forever. Alas, how it pains me! Since you did not let calamity disturb your peace, why should going and coming be a matter at all? You let go your hand and went, with no deliberation. Because you took vajra as your mind, you left a body that does not decay. I had disciples escort you back and settle you at Shuangjing. I heard the news and my heart was crushed; I looked toward Chang’an and shed tears. I wished to revere you in person in your niche, but the bonds of karma held me fast. I thought to return alive to comfort your spirit, and suddenly the years had passed a full twelve. It is not that this heart found any peace, only that conditions were not granted me. Lately I was fortunate to fulfill my original wish, and only then could set out these words in a eulogy. Alas, how it pains me! You have died, and I still live; I do not come, and you are not at peace. Our bodily forms differ, but we share this mind; the dark and the bright are sundered, yet in the end we shall be joined. I vow we shall return together and fulfill our deep pledge. In the still light shining, may you dwell at peace. I bow my head and pour out my grief and longing. I array fragrant viands and sprinkle sweet dew. At the moment of meeting, may you be willing to come. Light shines and illumines; I stand long in earnest waiting. Alas, may you enjoy the offering.
A Sacrificial Address for Great Master Yunqi

Alas! The Master was never born, nor does he go anywhere. He upheld himself by power and followed conditions; when the sea of desire surged with waves and the burning house blazed, the Master unrolled the wheel of his vow and came especially to rescue. He showed himself in the dust of toil and early returned to the compassionate father; once he mounted the road of enlightenment, he walked as a white ox steps. He looked on love as spittle and on kin as foes; those who swarmed like flies — who among them was not startled awake? He made the Dharma-realm his home and living beings his dwelling; he viewed self and things alike, with no two and no difference. He opened the gate of sweet dew and pointed the way to the Pure Land; scaled and shelled, feathered and furred, all at once rushed there. He grieved that the eye of the true Dharma was clouded at its precept-root, and with a vajra comb he scraped away grime and picked out darkness. The three thousand deportments and eighty thousand fine practices, at all times of day and night, he caused to be wholly pure. His person was the eyes of the multitude; his mind was the great house; and the foolish and crazed who came from the ten directions at once found rest. For more than forty years the Dharma-banner stood high; one rain moistened all alike, the herbs and the great trees. At a single drop, branches and leaves flourished together; and whoever obtained anything in the end accomplished it. I observe my Master as a lion king: he lies high in his lair and the herds run in panic. I observe the Master again as a healing-king tree: whoever draws near is sure to be cured of deep disease. Alas for our Dharma-ending age, the sun of wisdom long sunk; the Master in the long night held up the great lamp of wisdom. The Buddha is originally without mind; his mind was entrusted to the Master. The bodhisattva has no practice; practice was entrusted to the Master to uphold. Therefore the Master’s responding in the world was wholly without self; though he dwelt a hundred kalpas, what would be amiss? Alas! The Master appeared by condition and, condition ended, departed. We grieve for these blind multitudes who have lost their reliance. I come from a thousand li, holding a petal of incense, spreading out my five limbs in reverence to the still light. Master, your compassion is of one body with mine; because I am your kindred spirit, may you mirror my sincerity and come to receive the offering. Alas, may you enjoy it.
A Sacrificial Address for Jinzhu Xufang, the Master Lian

Alas! You bore the wheel of vow and were born in the realm of endurance. You early met an enlightened teacher and at once left love and affection behind. You aroused a firm and solid mind and repaid the debt of compassion. You cast your body into the empty mountains and endured hunger and cold. You reverently kept your teacher’s instruction and bore loads upon your own back. You aspired to offer to the ten directions, equal and unobstructed. You cut away thorns and made a monastery; you drove out foxes and hares and raised the Brahmā-chant. Monks came like clouds; gods and dragons guarded you. Rice piled up like a mountain, and those who came ate their fill, as much as they wished, like emptiness itself; those who stayed had no outside. You possessed the power of diligence and to old age did not slacken. Your one body was like a lodging, with not a thing clinging to it. I meant to join hands and go home together; how could I expect you to set out first and not wait? You lifted your hem and went — what a joyful release! You left the vajra banner, abiding and undecaying. The Dharma-body is clear and still; in the still light you are free. Only may your spirit not be darkened: mirror this deep sigh. Alas, how sorrowful! May you enjoy the offering.
An Essay on Forming a Society to Recite the Buddha’s Name, Practicing the Forty-Eight Vows and Being Born Together in the Pure Land

I bow before the truth that the Pure Land is only mind: every place is a way-place. Amitābha of self-nature is complete in every person. It is only that the dust of toil obscures and blocks, and men oppose self to other and right to wrong; hence earth and stones, mountains and hills are felt, and defilement and evil fill all. So the originally pure substance is hidden from the man before us, and his perfect wisdom and radiance do not appear in the least. All day his karmic consciousness is a vast blur; day after day the wind of objects blows wide. He knows only how to enjoy what is before him; who understands cultivating the cause for what lies after death? Therefore our Teacher in the Land of Bliss, Amitābha Buddha, aroused the mind on the causal ground, wearied of this endurance, and established forty-eight vows, each vow delivering beings; he cultivated the sixteen contemplations of mind, each mind becoming Buddha. He would have every person know that the mind is Buddha and not seek outside; would have each one understand that the vow itself is true and all return to self-nature. Push over the high mountain of self and other, and feel the jeweled ground level as the palm of a hand; shatter the illusory dream of the dust of toil, and be born on a lotus vast as a wheel. My mind being pure, that land is accomplished ready-made. Do not let yourself think of it only after the fact; bring the fruit to completion here and now. With no distinction of man or woman, all alike realize bodhi; whoever has the conditions all ascend to the jeweled ground. Yet Maitreya, though born of Heaven, still needed the prophecy at Vulture Peak; and Śākyamuni, of himself, still had to adorn a Buddha-land. Bitterly mindful that we live amid the five turbidities, our lives not to be kept for a moment, our evil karma manifold, and suffering hard to escape through long kalpas. Though father is kind and son filial, each can look only to himself; though elder brother loves and younger is respectful, how can one take another’s place? Even with wealth and honor and glory, in the end it is all one dream. Pondering this deeply, one is truly grieved to the heart. Therefore arouse the vow and cultivate the cause, resolved to settle it in this one life. Since you know all practices to be impermanent, how can you go on craving as before? Having awakened to the mind itself being Buddha, you need only take it up directly. To churn the long river into cream lies, after all, with the man himself; to turn the great earth into gold truly depends on oneself. I humbly pray that your vow-mind be like the Buddha’s — that is the Buddha-mind; that cause and effect be both true — you will surely attain the true fruit. Arouse one vow, and the four kinds of birth and the nine abodes will all leave the wheel of suffering together; give one drop, and the eight difficulties and three evil paths will all return to the Land of Bliss. The flower opens and you see the Buddha, fragrant as mother and child; delusion exhausted and the source regained, bright as ice and frost. One mind pure, the ten thousand virtues all return home; the great earth and its rivers and mountains all become the Land of Bliss itself.
A Sacrificial Address for Master Chekong of Mount Kuang

Your coming, Master — what matter, what purpose? Your going, Master — what mind, what concern? You appeared in the body of a bhikṣu and sat cutting off Heaven and Earth; you gave the lion’s roar and startled away foxes and hares. When you sought me on the cool mountain, clouds filled the streams and hills. And when you returned to your old hiding, the moon was full on your thatched door. You still held the pearl of nine windings, meaning to wait for me and cross over in secret. How could it be that in a single morning you set out on the long road, and the mournful news suddenly came? Alas! It leaves me with a mouth that cannot open, holding wrongs I cannot tell. For we were born together yet did not die together, returned together yet did not dwell together. But we rely on Mount Kuang’s height to cover all with the Dharma-body, and on the clear waters of Lake Peng to make the samādhi shine. Though the banner-pole has been toppled, we are fortunate that the exposed pillar has been set upright; and it suddenly makes the Five Elders call aloud and a thousand peaks all dance, the white deer grieve in the wind and the yellow dragon weep in the rain. Rolled up it is ever unrolled; the more you would hide it, the more it shows. This is to be praised and not lamented, to be laughed at and not wept over. Alas! Rest a while, Master, and hear this final word: break open the still light and overturn the Pure Land; come again, and if you meet a fierce and peppery acarya, he will grab you and never let you go back. Only may your spirit enjoy the offering.
A Brief Instruction Spoken Before the Mourning Curtain of the Layman Zeng Jiulong

On the twenty-sixth day of the fifth month of the thirty-sixth year of Wanli, on the day of the layman Zeng’s fifth-week observance, his fellow society members each raised incense and paid reverence, asking the monk Hanshan to give a brief instruction for the layman. Layman, do you hear? The Buddha said: all conditioned things are impermanent; they are a dharma of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing are ended, stillness and extinction are joy. Layman, do you understand? The layman dwelt in the world thirty-seven years, and all the conditioned things he did — at the very time of doing them, were they impermanent? Or impermanent after doing? Or is it only today that they are impermanent? If you say it is today that they are impermanent, that falls into annihilation. If you say they are impermanent after doing, then it need not wait for today. If they are impermanent at the very time of doing, then all the world is impermanent — why the layman alone? Layman, do you understand? If you understand that the doing is impermanent, then the impermanent has no nature of its own: who is it that arises and ceases? And one who neither arises nor ceases — how could he have birth and death? If the layman understands this, then today is precisely the time when he receives the joy of stillness and extinction; and those who grieve for him all hold views of arising and ceasing.
The Address for the Cremation of Master Da, Raising the Torch

The fire of the nature is true emptiness; the emptiness of the nature is true fire. Meeting on a narrow road, there is surely nowhere to dodge. I revere the Venerable Zibo, Great Monk Daguan: you came by chance into the human world and fell by mistake into the dust. Naked and bare you stripped off the cloth shirt your mother bore you in; shining and bright you revealed your original countenance. You shouldered the true Dharma with a shoulder refined to pure steel; you were utterly for others with a liver and gall cast from pig iron. On the road of death and life you went straight out and straight back; at the gate of present affairs it was half open and half shut. For more than sixty years your breast was pine wind and water moon; for seventeen hundred koans your staff was rabbit horn and turtle hair. Let him have the last word in elegance, still he could not help showing his head and hiding his tail. He dropped his stolen goods — who would have thought they would fall into the hands of the Hanshan Daoist? Today, before the assembly of gods and men, I hold them up in the full light. Does the great assembly see them? Raising the torch he drew the mark of a circle, saying: The staff pries open the clouds of the twin paths; from your whole body gushes the treasury of light. Take care, all of you, and look well: only now will you believe there is no obstruction.

A Hanging Mirror on the Śūraṅgama Sutra
Preface to A Hanging Mirror on the Śūraṅgama Sutra

The Śūraṅgama Sutra is the secret treasury of all Buddhas, the wondrous gate of cultivation, the root of delusion and awakening, the great source of the true and the false. What it expounds takes the one-flavored, pure, Tathāgata-garbha true mind as its substance. This mind-substance is of itself numinous and illumined, vast and clear, wide and empty and still, equal and thus, cut off from all names and marks. Sage and ordinary are one horizon; sentient beings and Buddhas are equal. Deluded, one has birth and death without end; awakened, the wheel of rebirth is at once stilled. Therefore our Buddha realized this and pitied beings for being deluded, and so borrowed a great expedient to open and reveal this teaching. He opened wide the gate of cultivation and realization and turned aside to show the road home. Thus all that the single scripture expounds, from beginning to end, is nothing but the two dharmas of delusion and awakening, true and false. Yet the road of delusion has ten thousand forms and awakening has many gates; if one would reach the substance and fathom the source, there is no lack of essentials. As for the method of going from delusion to awakening and the pointing that returns the false to the true, it lies precisely in the great samādhi of the Śūraṅgama and the wondrous gate of the three contemplations. If one wishes to see the Dharma-realm clearly, to penetrate one’s own mind through, and to return to the source at the very thing itself, nothing is more essential than this.

I sigh that its words are profound and its principles deep and hidden. Though the various commentators have finely and fully drawn out its meaning, students are greedy of the road and do not know the shortcut, so that contemplation of principle is obscured by stale words and cultivation loses right samādhi. Qing, not measuring his own narrowness, has long set his mind on this text, shutting off seeing and hearing and enduring ice and snow. But his wisdom and knowledge are dim; he does not presume to measure the sage’s mind rashly. Only at every thread of a through-road he roughly sets out his humble meaning, so that those who cultivate in hiding may be like one who takes up a mirror to see his form, and may at once, taking the matter at hand, set the mind at peace and suddenly melt into the treasury-nature.
Written by the mountain ascetic Deqing of Hanshan in the winter of the bingxu year of Wanli, at the Nārāyaṇa Cave on the Eastern Sea
A Hanging Mirror on the Śūraṅgama Sutra
Expounded by the Ming-dynasty śramaṇa of the Nārāyaṇa Cave on the Eastern Sea, Haiyin Shi Deqing
To Open the General Meaning, Two Chapters Are Set Forth (the detailed division into three parts is given in the General Discussion and is not listed here in full)
First, Opening Wide the Gate of Cultivation and Realization (from the opening request to the naming of the sutra)
Next, Turning Aside to Show the Differences of Delusion and Awakening (from the fine examination of the seven destinies to the fifty kinds of skandha-māras)

The first contains in brief four meanings: first, showing the substance of the three contemplations; second, showing the marks of the three contemplations; third, showing the function of the three contemplations; fourth, concluding the names of the three contemplations.

In first opening the gate of cultivation and realization there are four meanings. For the true source is clear and still, cut off from the tip of arising and ceasing; the Dharma-realm is deep and hidden, effacing the traces of sage and ordinary. Originally there is no cultivation or realization — how could it belong to delusion and awakening? Now, relying on the delusion that does not delude, one establishes the cultivation that does not cultivate, and so there is the realization that does not realize. For when one is deluded as to the true and chases the false, one sinks into the stream of birth and death. Now, wishing to return the false to the true, one must establish a practice that relies on the true. And this sutra takes the one-flavored, pure Dharma-realm, Tathāgata-garbha true mind as its substance. Relying on this one mind, one establishes the three contemplations; relying on these three contemplations, one returns to realize the one mind. Hence it is said: there is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm, and nothing that does not return to this Dharma-realm. Therefore Ānanda showed himself as one not yet awakened, not penetrating this mind, and so had long been much learned but had not attained the outflow-free, and could not at once pull out the root of birth and death; and so he was drowned in the trouble of Mātaṅga’s daughter. Thereupon he earnestly requested the wondrous gate of the three contemplations. So our World-Honored One first showed the one mind illumining the ten thousand dharmas, and first told him: the continuous succession of birth and death in all sentient beings comes solely from not knowing the permanently abiding true mind, the pure, luminous substance of the nature. And again he said: there is a samādhi named the Great Buddha’s Crown Śūraṅgama King, complete in all practices, the wondrous adorned road by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions go beyond through one gate. Seeing these two sayings, one may see the whole purport of the sutra. Is it not that he would have them first awaken to the one mind, rely on it to establish the three contemplations, cultivate these three contemplations, and return to realize the one mind? As for all that was answered thereafter, though there were many-sided decisions and winding examinations, they were nothing but a revealing of the source of the one mind and a secret setting forth of the substance of the three contemplations (from the first fascicle to the middle of the fourth). From this, entering upon practice and undertaking cultivation, he drew in the twenty-five sages to pass sideways through the methods of entry, and then selected the ear-root as precisely the first expedient (from the middle of the fourth fascicle to the beginning of the sixth). This is to let the beginner who first sets his mind know that the marks of contemplation are clear, and then let him entrust himself to the one mind, so that the dharmas naturally, of themselves, have the functions of cutting off delusion and realizing the true, high and low (from the beginning of the seventh fascicle to the middle of the eighth). When cultivation and cutting off are brought to their utmost, he then concludes by pointing to the gate of contemplation, so that beginning and end are one source and do not go beyond the great samādhi of the Śūraṅgama. So he ties it off with the sutra’s name. This is truly the great purport of the whole.

First, showing the substance of the three contemplations. This substance is what is called the permanently abiding true mind, the pure, luminous substance of the nature: that is, the one true Dharma-realm, the Tathāgata-garbha mind. It is shown first as the object contemplated, because one must rely on this substance to set in motion the function of great wisdom. Now this treasury-mind has three meanings: first, the empty Tathāgata-garbha; second, the non-empty Tathāgata-garbha; third, the Tathāgata-garbha that is both empty and non-empty.

First, the empty Tathāgata-garbha. It means that this treasury-nature has a substance that is originally empty, in which not one dharma is obtainable. It is like a maṇi jewel whose substance is empty and pure, utterly without form or mark; though it has colors according to direction, the colors do not leave the jewel, because they are the jewel itself. The true mind is originally pure, utterly cut off from false conditions; though it has the false according to conditions, the false does not leave the true, because it is the true itself. This is called true emptiness. Therefore for the contemplator one first shows the true mind as the substance of contemplation; the ability to contemplate this substance is called the contemplation of true emptiness (in the sutra it is named śamatha, also called the cessation that is substance-true). From the opening of the sutra, where Ānanda requests and the World-Honored One consents to speak, saying that there is a samādhi named the Great Buddha’s Crown Śūraṅgama King, complete in all practices, the wondrous adorned road by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions go beyond through one gate — from there onward, through the seven questions and eight arguments, he first decides the true and the false and says that the false is not the true, to make clear that the body and mind of the five aggregates do not exist and that the world is originally empty, breaking the two attachments to self and dharmas to reveal original enlightenment and true suchness; and so on to the three divisions and seven elements, all gathered back into the treasury-nature. Then true and false blend, and only then is it shown that the false is the true. From the shallow to the deep, the whole passage generally reveals the principle of the empty Tathāgata-garbha (from the request in the first fascicle to the end of the third).

Second, the non-empty Tathāgata-garbha. It means that this treasury-substance, though empty, possesses virtues equal to the Ganges’ sands that accord with the nature, containing and merging and absorbing all, leaving out not the finest detail. It is like a maṇi jewel whose substance, though pure, possesses the function of perfect illumining and can manifest all colors according to direction; the colors are the jewel, because the jewel manifests them. The treasury-nature, though empty, can manifest according to conditions the marks of the ten realms’ direct and circumstantial retribution; the marks are the nature, because the nature gives rise to them. This is called true non-emptiness. Therefore for the contemplator one shows this treasury-nature as the substance of contemplation; the ability to contemplate this substance is called the contemplation of non-emptiness (in the sutra it is named samāpatti, also called the cessation of expedient following of conditions). This begins with Pūrṇa’s clinging to marks and challenging the nature, the three kinds of continuity, deeply fathoming the cause of arising, fully clarifying the meaning of manifestation through karma, and generally revealing the substance of non-emptiness (from the beginning of the fourth fascicle to the half fascicle of text in this fascicle that ends with “therefore the wondrous, enlightened, luminous nature of true suchness is revealed,” some fifteen hundred words in all).

Third, the Tathāgata-garbha that is both empty and non-empty. It means that this treasury-nature has a substance that is pure and can respond and manifest. It is like a maṇi jewel whose substance is pure and perfect: being pure, it is not color, because it is the jewel; being perfect, it can respond, and is not no-color, because it is the color. Hence it is neither color nor jewel. And this treasury-nature, whose substance is pure and perfect: being pure, it is not mark, because it is the nature; being perfect, it can manifest, and is not no-mark, because it is the mark. Hence it is neither mark nor nature: this is called empty and non-empty. Because it is not mark, it is empty; because it is not nature, it is not empty. Neither identical nor separate, equal and thus, it is called the Middle Way. Therefore for the contemplator one shows this treasury-nature as the substance of contemplation; the ability to contemplate this substance is called the contemplation of the Middle Way (in the sutra it is named dhyāna, also called the cessation that is free of the two extremes and discrimination, also called even maintenance). This begins in the middle of the fourth fascicle with “the Tathāgata-garbha is not the mind,” and goes on to “permanent, joyful, self, pure,” in two chapters of text, nearly three hundred words.

Yet although the substance of the three truths above is not two, and to raise one is to raise all three, they are after all accompanied by words and names, and still retain successive distinctions; they have not reached the source of the one mind and are hard to fit with the purport of perfect fusion. Only when one is free of both identity and difference, and is precisely neither identical nor different, does the treasury-mind’s wondrous nature reach to the very bottom of the source and cut off all opposition. For truly, to be free of both is to efface both; to affirm both is to preserve both. Preserved, the three truths are numinously distinct; effaced, the one mind has no support. Stillness and illumination at once, preservation and effacement without obstruction: only one who forgets words can meet it in spirit, and only one who cuts off deliberation can penetrate it with the mind. It may be called a wondrous tally within the realm, an effacement identical with the Dharma-realm. Perfect fusion, perfect fusion; ponder it deeply, ponder it deeply — it is distinct and not obscured. Therefore when the Buddha had finished his exposition he summed up and told them: the principle of the treasury-nature spoken above is thus deep and wondrous; how could you, with the mind that knows, measure it, or enter it with worldly language? And this wondrous principle is complete in every person, yet though complete it is hidden and does not appear. It is like a lute: though it has a wondrous sound, without wondrous fingers it cannot be brought forth; though sentient beings possess the wondrous mind, without wondrous contemplation it cannot be revealed. And as I now have realized this true mind and dwell at ease in the great house, perfectly illumining the Dharma-realm, every movement is the great function appearing before me; but you are deluded as to it, and all your gestures and doings are the functioning of the dust of toil and karma. Hence it is said: when I press my finger, the ocean-seal gives forth light; when you for a moment raise your mind, the dust of toil rises first. There is no other reason for this than that you are unwilling to seek diligently and are content with a little. The man before him then asked: for what cause is there the false? He would show that the false is originally without cause, to make them understand that the false does not leave the true, and that it is also like the head, not to be obtained outside. Now this naturally wondrous nature is not made by cultivation; one need only turn the light back in a single thought to awaken to the jewel of the spirit being originally one’s own. So he concluded by rebuking idle disputation and earnestly urging cultivation and upholding, saying: though you remember and uphold the twelve divisions of the canon, it is not equal to a single day of cultivating the outflow-free work. Why deceive yourself and still keep your seeing and hearing, and not cultivate? Therefore when Ānanda heard this, his doubts dissolved, his mind awakened to true reality, and he asked to enter the jeweled house, to gather in and subdue his grasping, hoping to attain the dhāraṇī and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Seen thus, was not the whole of the exposition of the treasury-nature intended to have them first awaken to the one mind, rely on it to establish the three contemplations’ wondrous practice, and then, practice accomplished and understanding cut off, suddenly realize the one mind?
The first, showing the substance of contemplation, which belongs to the portion of seeing the Way, ends here.

Second, showing the marks of the three contemplations. Because of the previous exposition of the one true Dharma-realm, the Tathāgata-garbha mind, and because this mind-substance possesses the meaning of vast wisdom and radiance, it is called wisdom. Now with the wisdom that is the substance itself, one shines back upon the still and extinct substance; principle and wisdom are one suchness, free of thought and free of marks, and it is called the one mind-source, utterly without exposition. Now, by way of the gate of the true and the false, of arising and ceasing, to gather in the road that returns the false to the true, expedient devices are set up, and there are likewise three layers. Because wisdom illumines principle, the name “contemplation” alone is used; because it is made clear by way of the marks of the false, it is called the marks of contemplation.
Herewith a Brief Showing of the Gates of Contemplation
1. Śamatha: the Contemplation of Emptiness
2. Samāpatti: the Contemplation of Non-Emptiness
3. Dhyāna: the Contemplation of the Middle Way

First, śamatha, called the contemplation of emptiness. It means understanding that the one true Dharma-realm, the Tathāgata-garbha mind, is originally without arising and ceasing and without any marks. It is only because of a single thought of non-awakening that there is ignorance; and from this ignorance arise the three fine and six coarse marks, the four elements and six faculties, and all dharmas. Yet these dharmas are only what the mind manifests and are originally non-existent; they are but the one mind, whose substance is perfect and bright and free of all marks. Like the color in a jewel, they are originally non-existent, because they are empty. Hence it is said, “Form is emptiness”; and because form is not form, “form is not different from emptiness.” This is called true emptiness; one who contemplates thus is said to practice the contemplation of true emptiness.

Second, samāpatti, called the contemplation of non-emptiness. It means understanding that the faculties and body, the vessel-world and all dharmas, being the one mind, whose substance is perfect and bright, pure and naturally so, pervading the Dharma-realm and manifesting according to conditions — then all dharmas in their very substance are false and unreal, like an illusion. Like the color in a jewel, they appear clearly, and the whole jewel is the color; because it is the color, it is said, “Emptiness is form”; and because emptiness is not emptiness, “emptiness is not different from form.” This is called non-emptiness; one who contemplates thus is said to practice the contemplation of non-emptiness.

Third, dhyāna, called the contemplation of the Middle Way. It means relying on this still and extinct one mind to illumine all dharmas: all dharmas are naturally, in their very substance, still and extinct. Being still, they are called empty; being illumined, they are not empty. Like the jewel and its color, neither color nor jewel, it is called empty and non-empty. Neither still nor illumined, equal and thus, it is the one mind-source alone: clear and unmoving, free of identity and free of difference, precisely identical and precisely different, where the road of language is cut off and the reach of the mind is extinguished, where mind after mind leaves no interval, and one naturally flows into the ocean of sarvajñā. One who contemplates thus is said to practice the contemplation of the Middle Way.
Next, in the text that properly shows the marks of contemplation, the great divisions are four.
First, a general showing of the root of delusion and awakening; second, a proper showing of the marks of the one mind’s three contemplations.
Third, a brief showing of the method of untying the knots; fourth, an extensive showing of the first expedient.

First, the general showing of the root of delusion and awakening. Because Ānanda, hearing the Buddha’s exposition, had already awakened to the Tathāgata-garbha nature, the wondrously enlightened luminous mind, perfect and all-pervading, complete within himself and not to be sought outside. Yet because he had all along merely pursued grasping and could not gather it in and subdue it, and now wished to ponder and cultivate it without knowing the method of advance, he asked the question about entering the jeweled house, hoping to obtain a direct gate by which he might enter at once. Because one cultivates according to marks, this section is called the marks of the three contemplations. Yet what the World-Honored One showed had no other method: he first had him decide the true and the false clearly, and then treated him according to what was fitting. So if one would return the false to the true, the starting point is nothing but the two decisive meanings. For originally, being deluded as to this perfect, bright, clear and still true mind, one congeals it into the four elements and falsely divides it into the six faculties; faculties and dust join and falsely arise and cease, giving rise to the five turbidities and the functioning of karma and affliction, so that the wondrous perfect substance is walled off and does not penetrate — like many vessels set inside the great void. The clear and deep mind is muddied and loses its illumination, like sand and dust thrown into clear water. Thus it is that what was originally undivided becomes divided, and what was originally clear becomes turbid. Now if one would, right within arising and ceasing, realize the true and permanent, and turn the false and recover the wondrous enlightenment, one must first take this unborn and undying mind as the root of cultivation, and illumine and break through the source of arising and ceasing. Next one must examine the faculty that has been knotted, and see which is the root of affliction. If arising and ceasing enter the illumination, then here and now is the true and permanent; and if affliction knows its root, it splits at the touch of the blade. Then the one mind that illumines — mind after mind is still and extinct; and the ten thousand dharmas illumined — dharma after dharma is perfectly penetrating. Thus one leaps at once beyond the five turbidities and turns back to the one source. If one takes this as the causal mind, one can perfectly accomplish the fruit of realization. Yet though the one mind described is originally perfect and all-pervading, the six faculties that delude it have unequal power in the present. Now if one would awaken right within delusion and return home along the road, truly every gate can fathom the source and every place can join the ruts. But because the beginner’s mind is dim and inferior and does not understand perfect contemplation, one must point directly at what is before him, and the essential lies in entering deeply through one gate. Therefore he fully sets out the strengths and weaknesses of the six faculties and has him examine which is shallow and which deep. The shallow is contrary and separate and hard to penetrate; the deep is compliant and joined and easy to enter. If one can enter one and be without the false, then the six are clear and perfect, all falseness vanishes, and the one mind is pure. Thus the old possession of our own house can be recovered, and the nirvāṇa of all Buddhas can be realized.

After this he again questions the one and the six, intending to show that, clinging to the clear and still, the false arises, and to fathom deeply the root of arising and ceasing; then he raises again the doubt of the view of annihilation, and tests out the wondrous nature of the true and permanent. Here he has already secretly selected the ear-root as the first expedient for the beginner. If one single-mindedly guards the true and permanent and casts off arising and ceasing, then the supreme awareness will be perfected as the thought arises, and one will attain the sudden manifestation of the everlasting light, and arising and ceasing will be perfectly left behind. Then faculties, dust and consciousness will fall away in that very moment. This is truly the secret of perfect contemplation, the divine talisman for breaking the false, the purport of returning to the source. Its wonder lies here. This is what is meant by returning the false to the true, which goes beyond the two decisive meanings.

Second, properly showing the marks of the one mind’s three contemplations. Ānanda, hearing the second meaning-gate above — that arising and ceasing is the permanent — then raised the doubt as to what is called a knot and what is called release. His meaning was: arising and ceasing is impermanent and may be called a knot; now that it is permanent, what thing will be called a knot? And if the knot does not even exist, from what thing will release be named? For formerly he took the permanent as annihilation, and now he clings to the false as the true; both come from not understanding that delusion and awakening share one root and that the true and the false are one body, and hence this question. This is truly where the beginner is confused, and so it must be sifted and made clear, so that the marks of his contemplation may be distinct and he not fall into the views of emptiness or existence, and the purport of the Middle Way may be revealed and so fit the source of the one mind. Therefore all the Buddhas accordingly told him together: what makes your birth and death and nirvāṇa is entirely brought about by your six faculties. How could it admit any other thing? It is simply because of the division between delusion and awakening that there is the difference of knot and release. Though he spoke so plainly, the man before him still did not awaken; so the World-Honored One explained further: the nature of faculties, dust and consciousness is one and the same true source; bondage and release, the two roads, are originally without two different courses. For because of delusion as to the one true, one falsely sees the six faculties, and setting up knowing upon seeing and knowing is called birth and death; but understanding that the six faculties are originally one body, so that knowing and seeing are without seeing, that is nirvāṇa. This is truly the source of knot and release; how could it admit any other thing? Yet although this makes clear emptiness and existence, it has not reached the one mind. Why? Because the one true nature does not belong to birth and death or nirvāṇa; in the Tathāgata-garbha there is originally no coming or going, delusion or awakening. As for the conditioned arising and the unconditioned ceasing, both are produced by conditions, like the illusions before your eyes; and the unconditioned arising and the conditioned ceasing are entirely unreal, like the sky-flowers before your eyes. And since there is neither the true nor the non-true, how could there be a seer or a seen — the seer being the six faculties and the seen the six dusts? Moreover, between faculties and dust there is originally no real substance, only empty marks, and so they are like intertwined reeds. Therefore knot and release share one root, and sage and ordinary are not two. Just try to observe: in the intertwined, the nature of consciousness — that is, the eighth ālaya-consciousness — in emptiness, what name has it? For by the mutual dependence of clarity and dimness, the true and the false set each other up; deluded, the six falsenesses arise together; awakened, where does the one true rest? Truly, because this substance is most deep and subtle, its fumigation and transformation are beyond thought. Cling to it, and the true is no longer true; grasp it, and the non-illusory becomes illusory. And if one does not grasp it and it is not illusory, there is not even non-clinging; how then could the illusory dharma stand? Being thus, the six faculties are perfect and clear, emptiness and existence are both dispelled, the three truths are perfectly contemplated, and right and wrong are altogether effaced. Is not the purport of the wondrous perfect wholly here? This is called the vajra samādhi, the samādhi of illusion; cultivate it and one thought leaps beyond; intend it and all Buddhas realize it together. This is what is meant by “the Bhagavans of the ten directions, the one road of nirvāṇa’s gate.” If you would ascend straight to the other shore and go directly to the wondrous adornment, there is only this gate of the great samādhi; therefore you should cultivate it and realize and enter it.
Third, a brief showing of the method of untying the knots:

Above, the marks of the one mind’s three contemplations have been shown. This is the gate by which every Buddha accomplishes the Way. Now, wishing to ponder and cultivate it, one is thwarted because the beginner does not know the direct method; hence the question of the six untied and the one lost, which leads far on to the discussion of selection. Therefore our World-Honored One finely proclaimed the wondrous purport and skillfully showed the hidden mechanism, and for a moment knotted a flowered cloth into six knots, to make clear that relying on the one cloth there are six knots, and that when the knots are untied the cloth too does not remain; he would show that relying on the one true there are six falsenesses divided, and that when the false is dissolved the true too is not established. Why? Because in the realm of true purity there is originally no such thing: birth and death and nirvāṇa are both the marks of a flower of wild toil and inversion. Therefore one must forget both true and false before one can return to the Middle Way and go straight to the source of the one mind. So, following the request for the method of untying the knots, he examined and made clear the place to set to work: to undo the knot at the very center to show that the two extremes have no strength, and to enter directly in the full light — one must reap the fruit in the Middle Way. This is truly the essential art of entering the perfect and the sharp tool for breaking delusion. Only, the Dharma-gate is most deep and one fears it is hard to believe firmly; therefore the World-Honored One swore to it, saying: what I speak is the subtle cause and condition of the world beyond, not the coarse marks of worldly concord. Moreover in all my mundane and supramundane dharmas I have understood every cause; how much more in this cultivation should I not know its joints and essentials? With such a function, one need not labor a finger’s snap to realize the unborn at once, nor traverse a journey to ascend straight to Buddhahood. Therefore, Ānanda, choose according to your own mind: whichever faculty you rely on, undo it with this wondrous art, and what falseness need you fear will not be destroyed? But I fear you cannot leave at once by perfect contemplation, and so must dissolve it step by step: first choose one faculty as the first expedient. If this faculty is untied at the start, the five other adhesions fall away with it, and you first attain the emptiness of the person. From there the wisdom of contemplation increases in clarity, and thereafter one accomplishes liberation from dharmas. If the person and dharmas contemplated are both empty, then the wisdom of the contemplation that empties them is also effaced. This is truly medicine and disease both sent away, the true and the conventional both fused, the three truths numinously distinct, and the one mind without support. Such perfect illumination naturally tallies with the hidden pivot in the dark. This is called realizing the unborn from samādhi and realizing the permanent joy right in the six faculties. Of direct pointers there is none higher than this. Is not the wonder of the beginner’s expedient here?

Fourth, an extensive showing of the first expedient (all twenty-five sages are each the first expedient, but only Guanyin’s single gate of the ear-root fits the faculties of this world, and so it is called an extensive showing):

Ānanda, hearing the previous exposition, had the marks of contemplation clearly and had awakened to the fact that one may realize entry through any faculty; yet he still did not know the method of setting to work and doing the practice wherever one may be, nor had he understood the precise pointing out of which faculty is fit to be the fitting vessel for this world and the first expedient. And he was about to fix his will on advance and cultivation in hope of accomplishing the fruit of the Way, that he might not fail this good assembly or betray the secret words, and also for the far benefit of the future and the accomplishment of the final exposition. Hence the question asking for the gift of the secret and adorned. Yet the purport of this secret and adorned is the fundamental Dharma-gate of our Buddha’s own realization, most deep and subtle, hard to understand and hard to ponder; the ocean of fruition is beyond words, utterly without exposition. Now he bends down to point it out, and it must be done by way of the sideways; therefore he borrows the twenty-five sages, each telling his own first expedient. His meaning is to show that the three divisions and seven elements can all be returned to the source wherever one is, and that the great and small of the three vehicles, far and near, may all press in together. And he would have them believe firmly without doubt, taking this as their evidence. Therefore the sages came forward in turn, using their own first ascent: some analyzed form or understood form to take the single true; some, right within the conventional, left the conventional to return to the Middle Way. Partial and perfect exchanged places, stars and moon interlaced; shallow and deep drove on together, oxen and sheep crossed over as one. Thus every gate is always the perfect penetration, and every dharma becomes liberation. If one can enter this samādhi and realize this wondrous gate, then wherever one is the everlasting light shines everywhere, and as the thought arises all Buddhas appear before one; water flowing and wind moving together proclaim the perfect sound, and the world’s mountains and rivers all manifest samādhi. Only then does one know that self and other are not two, that direct and circumstantial retribution merge into one another, that habitual outflows are dissolved in a flash and the many dusts are cleared in a single thought; the practice of non-doing spreads abroad, and the joy of the true and permanent appears of itself. Yet this sharp tool of the secret and adorned, given to a bold great man, what hardness will it not break, what knot will it not untie? But though the direct and the partial are both reached and compliance and opposition both penetrate, one does not know which is the essential wonder as the fitting root for this world. To be master amid the dust, without great wisdom one cannot keep one’s eyes lowered; to seize the honor in the midst of noise, without great compassion one cannot set to work. Therefore Mañjuśrī came to select which fits the faculties of this world, and it is Guanyin’s ear-root alone that can serve as the first expedient. Why? Originally the ocean of enlightenment is clear and perfect, its perfect clarity primevally wondrous; there is originally no world and no sentient beings at all. It is only that a single thought has just arisen, and bubbles in the void at once appear, and as conditions do not cease, the three existences all arise together. Thus the six places are falsely divided and the many dusts falsely separated, so that the perfect-penetration wondrous substance cannot be perfect and penetrating and the permanently abiding true mind cannot permanently abide. If one takes the false dharmas as wholly true, then the nature of returning to the source is not two; but alas, the faculties are not the same, and so the road of expedients has many gates. For the sagely nature, compliance and opposition both penetrate; for the beginner there is no lack of slowness or speed. Now if one enters by way of the six dusts, the substance of the six dusts is originally not permanent; if one relies on the five faculties to enter, the nature of the five faculties does not touch the perfect fusion; if one relies on the six consciousnesses, the six consciousnesses are plainly arising and ceasing; if one borrows the five great elements, the five great elements are without knowing and dull and dim; if one relies on the nature of seeing, though it gathers in all six faculties, it still remains within the seer and the seen and has not forgotten illumination; if one contemplates the nature of consciousness, though it contains the ten thousand dharmas, it still retains discrimination and is hard to fit with the true. Now if one would truly fit the teaching-substance of this world and precisely show what suits the faculties, and quickly take samādhi, one must truly enter by hearing. Why? Because the root of hearing is perfect and wondrous: it hears everywhere in ten places; the place of hearing is empty and fused, and walls cannot separate it; sounds arise and cease, but the nature of hearing is everlasting; waking and sleeping are one suchness, beyond the reach of body and mind. Thus one can realize the true and permanent by way of the nature of hearing, and enter the wondrous enlightenment from the ear-root. Moreover, the beings of this world have this faculty the sharpest: for pointing out what suits the faculties, nothing surpasses it. Truly, because they are deluded at the root and follow sound, they turn and flow through birth and death; if one can reverse the stream and be without falseness, will one not at once fit with the unborn? This is the vajra samādhi, the wondrous gate of illusion; being thus secret, it absolutely requires true cultivation. Why not use hearing to hear one’s own hearing? How could one be willing to store up hearing and make of it a fault and error? And hearing has no substance of its own: it is named from sound. If one turns back the false and leaves the dust, what name or form has the nature? This is why, when one faculty returns to the source, the six faculties are all liberated. And as for the six faculties’ illusory film and the three realms’ sky-flowers: now hearing is restored and the film removed, so dust dissolves and awareness is pure; when purity is at its utmost, light reaches everywhere, and still illumination contains the void. Faculties and objects are both empty, like a dream; how could the objects in a dream keep your bodily form? Generally, the men and women of the world are all made by illusion out of illusion; though they seem to move and shake, it is all the pulling of a single mechanism. If the mechanism rests and the illusion dissolves, then feeling is forgotten and clinging falls away, and the perfect, luminous, wondrous substance appears on the spot, and all Buddhas and sentient beings are in that moment equal. Such is the wondrous benefit, truly perfect penetration. Why not reverse the inverted mechanism of hearing, turn the hearing back upon its own true nature, and so accomplish the unsurpassed Way? This is the single wondrous gate of the Buddhas numerous as motes of dust, the shortcut of cultivation of the sages and worthies of the three times. It is not Guanyin’s alone: I too have realized entry through it. So for those who would rescue the final kalpa and seek to escape birth and death, who wish to accomplish bodhi quickly, nothing surpasses the ear-root. This is the gate shared by great and small, the dharma spoken alike to shallow and deep. Only cultivate according to this, and you will surpass the remaining faculties; of true essentials of mind, none is more wondrous than this. Thereupon the man before him, hearing this, understood his own mind clearly, plainly saw the road home and the way of returning to the true — the marks of contemplation were clear and there was no confusion before him. But alas, in the future Dharma-ending age, false ways will confound the true; how shall those who believe and practice according to the teaching gather in the mind, keep the rules, attain right fumigation and cultivation, establish the way-place and keep far from all māra affairs? Therefore he aroused the request to deliver others, to benefit far the faculties of the future and to comprehend the long road. Yet this still belongs to the affairs of the gate of practice. And what the World-Honored One answered has no other method: he directly takes the three decisive meanings within the Vinaya — namely, gathering in the mind by the precepts, from which samādhi and wisdom are born; when these three are perfect and clear, one can surpass all outflows. Now in the previous seeing of the Way and clarifying of the mind, the nature of wisdom has already been opened; and in the expedients of cultivating the Way, the marks of samādhi are perfect and clear. But as for the precepts being the foundation, this has not yet been plainly stated. Now if one would attain right fumigation and cultivation, one must rely on samādhi and wisdom; and if one would go against the prohibitive precepts and practices, one must receive the wheel of the precepts. Moreover the sea of birth and death floods the heavens, beginning from a single thought of a brimming cup; the forest of affliction blots out the sun, born from a sprouting root. Now if one would cut off the branches and stop the flow, the essential lies in damming the source and pulling out the root. Though the precepts have many categories, the four grave ones are the root; when the root does not arise, the branches and streams cease of themselves. Yet true cultivation takes freedom from desire as its root, and so unchastity is punished first, as the first of birth and death. Because mutual debt and injury drag one on, next come killing and stealing. And as one raises false words to boast before the world, craving secretly grows; and if one fully discusses the repayment of debts, killing and stealing are alike, for they forever destroy the good roots and prevent samādhi. Therefore they are classed together as grave faults and must all be cut off. If one would perfectly accomplish the study, one must first uphold this ice-clear purity; and if one can leave none of the four matters undone, one will naturally keep far from all māra affairs, right practice can be accomplished, and right samādhi can be entered. Yet though present conduct is easy to control, old habits are hard to remove; therefore one must recite the heart-mantra of my unsurpassed Buddha’s Crown. This is the double cultivation of the manifest and the secret and the joint operation of the three wisdoms, whereby the three obstructions can be broken, the three delusions removed, the three realms surpassed and the three bodies realized. Moreover the power of this divine mantra is swift and secretly sustaining: one need only apply it according to the teaching, and it breaks delusion as frost meets the sun. Therefore I briefly set out the rules, that one may rely on a pure teacher; and if one would know the way-place in full detail, one must make all conditions complete and purify both body and mind, cultivating matter and principle together, so that one may in a matter of days take bodhi and in a fixed term accomplish the holy fruit. The practice of the wondrous perfect truly lies here. Is not the essential of returning to the true here? Therefore he proclaims the divine mantra and causes the assembly all to hear it, fully revealing its power and urging them to firm belief, thus completing the gate of cultivating the Way and gathering in the whole of the wondrous perfect practice.
